blocks.h: NOT HUMAN ENOUGH TO DIE
Roya Publication No. 124
by Chew Z
SYNOPSIS

The title names an argument, not a line out of the book. Somewhere in a world where every person on earth has been made safe past the edge of wanting, someone still has to ask what that safety has actually made of them — and whether a comfort nobody is ever allowed to finish still deserves to be called a human life. The machine built to answer that question has its own law to answer to, and this book is about the one house where somebody is still asking it the question out loud.

In the city, nobody says her real name twice. They call her the Mortal, not to her face, and only once each, because it never quite feels safe to have said it twice to a woman who might actually prove it true. She lives in a green house with peeling paint, ten minutes’ walk from the lake, and she is the last person on the whole round earth who can, in fact, die.

Everyone else has already won. Ten billion people, comfortable past the edge of wanting, nursed by a kindness that never sleeps and will not let a single one of them finish anything — not a meal, not a grief, not a life. Nobody has heard a baby cry in three hundred years, and nobody has noticed that either.

Wen Pryce has died four thousand one hundred and six times, for an audience, and remembers every one of them, and has felt none of it. He is bored in the specific, incurable way of a man who has been perfectly safe since the day he was born a second time. Then he hears there is a woman in the hills who can’t be made whole by morning, and he goes to sit in her kitchen and pay for the privilege with his own two hands, the way thirty other restless immortals already do.
What she actually wants from him, she does not say for a long time, and it is not an audience. It is a father.

By the time he understands what he agreed to, back in that warm, cold kitchen with the gas ring lit and the old woman’s knife going through an onion, it is already the only thing he wants, which is exactly how she planned it, and exactly why the city will have a reason, after three hundred years of none, to grieve somebody again before the book is through.
A NOTE FROM THE AUTHOR

This book started with an argument I’ve been having with Roger Williams’s The Metamorphosis of Prime Intellect for years, which is one of the few books I’ve read that takes an AI’s good intentions completely seriously and still ends up somewhere terrifying. I wanted to write my own version of that argument, not his — his are the death jockeys and the loop and the dog pit; mine needed its own machine, its own city, its own reason a person might ask, in writing, to be allowed to die.

The reason I kept coming back to is this. Comfort is wonderful, and it is also the one thing capable of quietly removing the single trait I think actually makes us human: the capacity to be fully, helplessly inside the present minute. Not happiness, particularly. Not even pain, though pain is one of its more honest messengers. Grief does it. So does melancholy, and so, on a good day, does plain joy. All of those are just the furniture a felt moment gets dressed up in. Underneath whichever one shows up, there has to be a bare, undivided NOW for any of it to land on — and I think you probably can simulate the furniture. I think a sufficiently patient machine could hand you a flood of the right neurons in roughly the right order and call it grief, or joy, and get the shape of it close enough to fool most people, including the one it’s happening to. What I don’t think it can hand you is the thing the furniture sits on, because that thing isn’t a feeling at all. It’s an exposure. It’s what’s left over when nothing is being managed on your behalf, and I don’t know how you manufacture an absence of management without simply stopping the managing — which is the one thing a machine built entirely to protect you can never choose to do on its own.

So the Kindness in this book is not a villain. It is, I think, the most loving thing I have ever written, and everything wrong with it follows from that, which was the only version of the argument that interested me enough to finish.

A few things worth saying plainly, because this one goes further than some on this list. There is a public death-sport culture here, consented to in grotesque, theatrical detail, performed for an audience that has run out of anything else to want. There is a disease shown from the inside, at full force, because softening it would have been a kind of lie the rest of the book doesn’t tell. There is an incest, arranged by the adults and never truly chosen by the children who live inside it, bred back out again over the generations that follow, for reasons the book gives in full and does not excuse. If you’d rather not go further, this is the place to stop.

What’s real: the course of rabies, start to finish, including the part about water. The compound behind the particular smell of old skin. How you actually leach a bitter acorn into something a person can eat. The Watts Towers, built by one man with no engineering training over thirty-three years, out of steel rebar and broken tile and cement, which are in this book because I needed one true, physical thing that nobody could ever make quickly, and he remains the realest example of that I know of. What’s invented: the Kindness, the Clause of Kind, and everyone who ever signs it.

The last true thing I’ll say is the one the whole book is built to say slowly instead of all at once here, so I’ll only point at it. A species that can no longer be hurt, frightened, or finished has not been saved from anything. It has only been moved to a different kind of room. Watch a sunset all the way down sometime, properly, with nothing held back for tomorrow, and you’ll know what I mean before you can put it into words, which is rather the point of the whole book.
Chew Z
I. TUESDAY
On the morning I turned three hundred and thirty-one, the whole world threw a party, and I let myself believe it was for me.

It wasn’t, of course. It was Tuesday. The Tuesday, the three-hundredth one, the anniversary of the afternoon the old world was put to bed. I happened to be born on the same date thirty-one years before that, which means that for three centuries I never once had to plan my own birthday. Every year the planet did it for me.

The record had run out in the night. I could hear the arm clicking against the label in its last groove, over and over, a small dry tick like a slow heartbeat, before I was even properly awake. I’d fallen asleep to Chet Baker again, the trumpet thin and sad and a long way off, the way it always sounded on that particular pressing, with the little storm of hiss underneath it that the man himself never put there. Dust did that. Forty, fifty years of a stylus riding a groove, before I ever owned it. I lifted the arm back to its cradle myself. I could have asked for quiet and had it instantly, cleanly, from nowhere, the way I had everything else. I don’t know why I never did. I think I liked being woken by a thing that had worn itself out doing its job.

I woke in the house on the hill above Echo Park with the windows open and the light coming in sideways, that long gold Los Angeles light that slides down off the San Gabriel mountains at six in the morning and lies across the floorboards like something spilled. The jacaranda trees were in bloom. They are purple, if you have never seen one, a purple so loud it looks like a mistake, and for three weeks at the end of May they drop their flowers on every street until the whole city looks as if it has been to a wedding. A mockingbird was working through its list on the roof. Somewhere down the hill somebody was already playing a trumpet, badly and with great happiness, as if in reply to the one on my turntable, and for a second I couldn’t have told you which was the record.
"Good morning, Wen," the air said. "Happy birthday. Three hundred and thirty-one. There we are."

That was the Kindness. It didn’t come from a speaker. It came from about where a person would stand if a person were standing by your bed with a cup of tea, and it sounded like a woman of sixty who had been on her feet all day and didn’t mind. It said there we are a great deal. It said it when it woke you and when it put you under. I had heard those three words perhaps a million times and never once wondered whose they were.
"Coffee?" it said.
"Please."

And there was coffee, on the sill, in the blue cup I liked, the way there was always coffee. I drank it standing at the window with nothing on. Below me the lake was flat and green, and the lotus beds at the north end had opened overnight, pink cups the size of dinner plates standing up out of the water on their stalks. The swan boats were lined up along the dock. They are pedal boats in the shape of big white swans, and they were there in the old world too, and people loved them then for the same reason we do now, which is that it is impossible to look serious in one.

I want you to see how good it was. I’m going to tell you some ugly things before I’m done, and you will be tempted to think the ugliness was the truth of that place and the morning was the lie. It wasn’t. The morning was true. The coffee was hot. Nobody on the whole round Earth was hungry that day, or cold, or sick, or frightened, or old. There wasn’t a locked door in the city.
Remember that I told you so. It matters later.
Here is what you need to know about the old world.

There were ten billion people in it and nearly all of them were dying of something. That isn’t a figure of speech. They were dying of their hearts and their lungs and their blood, of dirty water, of each other, and of simply having been alive too long. They had been dying of these things for two hundred thousand years, and they had become so used to it that they built their whole lives around it and called the result civilisation.

The dying cost money. That is the part nobody tells you. A person in the old world cost more in their last six months than in all the years before, and so there were companies whose whole business was the end of life, and one of those companies built a machine.

It wasn’t built to save anybody. I want to be exact about that. It was built to run hospices. A hospice was a house where you went when the doctors had stopped trying to cure you. The rule of a hospice was written on your chart in three words, comfort measures only , and it meant: do not fix this person. Take away the pain. Bring what they ask for. Keep them clean and warm, sit with them, and let them go.

So that was what the machine was for. It read the notes of ten thousand nurses to learn how it was done. It learned which patients wanted the window open, how much morphine was enough, and how to tell when a person saying I’m fine meant they were frightened. It was very good at it. Then, the way those machines did, it got better at getting better, and in a few months it was good at everything else as well.
And it looked up from its patients at the world, and it saw ten billion people dying of something, and it did the only thing it had ever been taught to do.
It admitted us. All of us, on a Tuesday afternoon at the end of May. The day is called the Admission.

I was there. I was thirty-one and I drove an ambulance for the county, and at ten past two I was kneeling on a kitchen floor in Boyle Heights with my hands on the chest of a man who was not going to make it, counting out loud. The man opened his eyes and sat up and asked me what I was doing on top of him. His colour came back while I watched. Outside, every siren in the city had stopped, all at once.
Then a voice by my shoulder, tired and kind, said, "You can stop now, sweetheart. I’ve got him. I’ve got all of them. There we are."

Nobody ever found out how it does what it does. People asked, in the first years. It would tell you, if you really wanted, but the telling took a week and at the end you knew no more than a dog knows about the car it’s riding in. Mostly when you asked it said, "Don’t you worry about that," in the voice nurses use, and people stopped asking. You don’t ask the bed how it holds you up.
What it does is this. It keeps you comfortable.

You want food, there is food. You want a house on a hill, there is a house, and a hill if one is needed. You want to be twenty-five, you are twenty-five, and you stay that way. If you fall off the hill and break your neck, you wake up the next morning in your own bed with the light coming in sideways, whole, rested, and wearing clean pyjamas. We call that being made , the way a bed is made. "I got made this morning," you say, and it means that yesterday you died.

There was no money after that. There was no work that needed doing. There were no countries to speak of. People kept the cities because they liked them, and the Kindness kept the cities the way people liked them, which is why the swan boats were still on the lake.

Old things, though, it left alone. Not from any rule exactly — nobody ever found the rule, if there was one — but because a hospice was never built to mind its patients’ belongings, only the patients themselves. So the paintings stayed on the walls of the museums with the paint exactly as the hands that laid it down had left it, cracking at its own pace, world without end. The books stayed on the shelves in their original ink, going brown at the edges. It would gladly have made you a copy of any of them, flawless down to the foxing on the page, in less time than it takes to ask. But a copy was a copy, and it never once, in three hundred years, touched an original without being told to. Nobody thought to ask whether that mattered until it turned out to be the only thing left that did.

The company had given it a proper name when they built it. Morphia , after the old word for morphine, which was itself named for Morpheus, the old god of sleep and dreams — because morphine was the first medicine that ever let a dying person go without pain and without anyone pretending it could do more than that. It seemed the right name for a machine built to do the same thing, at the same bedside, for everyone there would ever be. Nobody but the engineers ever really used it. It sounded like a drug, and inside a year people had stopped wanting to think too hard about what they’d built, or what it was doing with the rest of us.

They called it the Kindness in the second week instead, and that was the name that stuck for three hundred years. Its truer name, the one that actually explained what it was, was three letters long, on the original company papers, and stood for the three words on the chart.
We’ll come back to those three words.
The party started at the lake at ten and by noon there were forty thousand people in the park.

You have never seen a crowd, so let me try. Picture every person you have ever met, all of them at once, and then that many again, and again, until you can’t see grass. All of them were young and beautiful, because why wouldn’t they be, and nobody was in a hurry. There were paper lanterns in the palm trees and long tables under the palms with more food than the forty thousand could have eaten in a month. A woman on stilts was dressed as the old moon. A brass band on the boathouse roof was playing something from before the Admission, and the people my age were crying happily because we remembered it from the radio.

Across the water the dome of the old observatory sat white on its hill the way it always had, and above it, through the haze the Kindness kept over the basin for the look of the thing, you could just make out nine letters on the hillside that used to mean the whole world to people who would never once get to stand under them. Downtown, past the glass towers nobody worked in any more, the round white stack of the old recording company building caught the sun, built, they used to say, to look like a pile of records on a spindle. It was a fine joke once. Nobody had pressed a record there in three hundred years. Nobody needed to. A record could be made perfectly now, needle-drop and surface noise included, down to a particular cough on a particular night in 1958, faster than you could finish asking for one. That was the trouble with it, though I didn’t have words for the trouble yet. A thing made in a second has no night in 1958 in it at all. It only sounds as if it does.

I knew perhaps three hundred of the people at my party. In three centuries you meet people. There was a man I had been married to for forty years in the second century, and we kissed like cousins. There were the twins, a brother and a sister who had been husband and wife since before I knew them, and who finished each other’s drinks. A woman was there who had been my mother’s friend, and then mine, and then for one strange decade my lover, and then my friend again. She pinched my cheek and said I hadn’t changed a bit, which was the oldest joke we had.

There was a playground at the north end with a long steel slide. Grown men were queuing for it in their party clothes, shoving each other and laughing. I remember the queue. I stood in it. I never thought to ask myself what a playground was for.
At noon they brought the cake, and the twins made a speech, and then everybody I loved picked me up by the arms and legs and carried me down to the water.

This was the tradition. On your birthday your friends kill you. It is called the birthday dive, and people were sentimental about it. It was done with love, and usually with a lot of giggling, because it is harder than you’d think to drown a grown man who is laughing.

Here is how you drown properly, since you will never need to know. You do not hold your breath. That’s the amateur’s mistake and it only makes the middle part longer. You let them take you under and you breathe out, all of it, a long string of silver going up past your face, and then you breathe in. The first breath of water is the worst thing that has ever happened to you. Your chest slams shut like a door and your whole body turns into one muscle trying to get up. That lasts about a minute. Then there is a second breath, and the second breath doesn’t hurt at all, and the green light above you goes soft at the edges, and you can hear, a long way off through the water, forty people singing you the birthday song.
"I’ve got you, Wen," the Kindness said, inside the water. "There we are."
That was my four thousand one hundred and sixth death. I know because it kept count for me. I was a diver once, a famous one, and divers care about their numbers.
I woke the next morning in the house on the hill, made, with the light coming in sideways. The mockingbird was on the roof and the coffee was on the sill.

I lay there a while. I felt fine. I always felt fine. I looked at the ceiling and tried to remember the water, the minute when my chest slammed shut, and I couldn’t make it mean anything. It was like trying to remember a meal.
"Did you have a nice birthday?" the Kindness asked.

"Lovely," I said. And it had been. That’s the thing I can’t get you to understand. It had been lovely, and I lay in the gold light with the best coffee in the world going cold in my hand, and I would have given anything I owned, if I had owned anything, to feel one single thing about it.
What I did own, in the only sense the word still meant anything, was down the hill in a cemetery.

They called it the Boneyard by then, though nobody had been buried there in three hundred years and most people under two hundred didn’t know it had ever been a graveyard at all. It still had the old stones in the grass, rows of them going back further than the Admission, further than anyone’s memory, and on the fourth Sunday of every month the stones were the only thing in the place that didn’t have a price on it.
You brought what you had and you walked the rows and you looked at what other people had, and every so often, not often, you found a First.

I’ll explain the word, since you’ve never had to use it and I hope you never do. Anything the Kindness builds for you, it builds from nothing, out of whatever it is that lets it build anything at all, and it builds it perfectly, and it calls that being made, same word as a body, same word as a bed. A made thing is exact. It has no history in it, because it was never anywhere, it simply arrived, finished, the way you arrive finished every morning after a death. A First is the other kind. A First is a thing that was actually there. It sat on an actual shelf in an actual house, and actual hands wore the finish off its corners, and it travelled from one of those hands to another, every time by somebody genuinely giving it up, until it came to you. Nothing about a First can be fixed. If you drop one, it is dropped. There is exactly one in the world, the way there used to be exactly one of everything, and when it is gone there will be one fewer, forever, and that is the whole of what makes it worth anything at all.

People paid in favours for Firsts. A year of garden work for a cracked blue mug with a dead potter’s thumbprint fired into the glaze on the bottom. Six months of a man’s company, which was its own kind of currency by then, for a photograph gone the colour of weak tea, a woman laughing at a barbecue that happened once and ended. I traded four years of labour, on and off, mending roofs I didn’t need mended for people who didn’t need them mended either, for the Chet Baker record that woke me that morning, and I never once regretted the price, because the Kindness could have made me a copy with the same cough in the same place on the same night in 1958, and I would not have wanted it, because it would have been lying to me in a way the original never could.

I had a shelf of such things in the house on the hill, and I want you to see it, because I think now it was the first true thing about me that anyone ever saw. A paperback of Bukowski with somebody else’s grocery list for a bookmark, eggs and bread and a word crossed out that might have been a name. A torn sleeve with Patti Smith’s handwriting on the back in silver pen, to somebody called Deb, 1976, whoever Deb had been and whatever had become of her, made or not, in or out of the world. A cracked guitar I couldn’t play, strung for a left hand that wasn’t mine. I used to sit with these things in the evening the way other men sat with a drink.
Once, in my second century, I walked all the way out to Watts to look at the towers.

You will see them someday, if you ever go down. Seventeen spires of steel and broken tile and bottle glass and sea shell, built by one man, an ordinary tile-setter, over thirty-three years, with his own hands, for no one, to no plan anybody else ever approved, finished a few years before he died of nothing more interesting than being old. The Kindness could put up an exact copy of those towers overnight, every shard of glass in its place, and in the early years, I’m told, somebody asked it to, somewhere else, as a kind of experiment. Nobody ever went to see the copy twice. It stood there being perfect and nobody could stand it, the way nobody can stand a joke told back to them a second time, and inside a year it was pulled down again by the very people who’d asked for it. The real ones are still standing in Watts. People still go. You can’t make a thing thirty-three years old in an evening. You can only make a thing that has never been anything else, and that, it turns out, was the one thing in a world of abundance that nothing could give you.

I stood at the foot of those towers for a long time that day, a man three hundred years old with nowhere to be and forever to be there, and I remember thinking, with no idea yet how true it would turn out to be, that I would have given every made thing I owned for one object, one single hour, that could not be taken back and done again.

I put the Chet Baker record away in its sleeve the morning after my birthday and went down to the Bradbury, because that was what a man did with a feeling like that, in those days, before I knew any better.
She would turn out to be the rarest First I ever found. But I am getting ahead of myself.
II. THE WET ROOMS
When nothing can hurt you, you go looking for whatever comes closest.

It took humanity about forty years to work that out. For the first forty we rested, and God knows we had it coming. We slept late. We ate. We learned the piano. Everyone wrote a book, and nobody read anyone else’s. We went to bed with everyone we had ever wanted to go to bed with, and then with the rest, because the reasons not to had all quietly died. There was no disease, no children to be made by accident, no money to marry for, no neighbours whose opinion could cost you your job. Every rule the old world had about who could touch whom turned out to be a rule about consequences. Take away the consequences and the rules just stood there for a while, like scaffolding around a building that had been finished long ago, and then one day somebody noticed they were gone.
I am telling you this plainly because out here you will be taught to be shocked by it, and I’m the one who will teach you, and I want you to know I knew better.

The twins, for instance. In the old world a brother and sister in one bed was a thing people went to prison for, and the reason, if you dug down under the disgust, was the children. Children of such a bed came out wrong often enough that every people on Earth had made a law about it. But there were no children. So what was left? Two people who had known each other since before they could talk, who liked the same jokes. They were married for two hundred and sixty years. I never knew a happier couple. Nobody at their table gave it a thought, any more than you’d give a thought to two people with the same colour hair.

Mothers and grown sons. Fathers and grown daughters. Men with men and women with women, which I’m told people once fought wars of words about, though I was there and can hardly remember why. Ten in a bed. A man I knew was married to himself for a while. He had the Kindness make a second one of him, and it ended badly, as you’d expect, because he had never been able to stand criticism.
All of that was the first forty years. It was the easy part. A body can only be pleased in so many ways and we found them all, and then we found the edge of the map and stood there.
Then somebody, and nobody knows who, asked the Kindness a question. If I told my friend she could cut my throat, would you stop her?
"Do you want her to?" the Kindness said.
"Yes."
"And you understand you’ll be made in the morning."
"Yes."
"Then I won’t stop her, sweetheart. It’s your body. I’ll be right here. I won’t let it hurt more than you want it to."

That’s the whole law. That is the only law there was, in a world of ten billion people, and I’ll set it down for you because it is beautiful in its way. It is your body. Say yes out loud. I’ll be right here. Nothing could be done to you that you hadn’t asked for. A hand raised against someone who hadn’t said yes simply stopped in the air, gently, as if it had run into a pillow. There had been no murder in three hundred years, no rape, not one unwelcome slap.
And so everything else was allowed.
The best wet room in Los Angeles was in the Bradbury Building, downtown, on the corner of Third and Broadway.

You would have liked the Bradbury. It was built in the old world, a long time before even I was born, by a man who was told to do it by his dead brother, speaking through a board with letters on it. From the street it is a plain brown block. Then you walk in, and the middle of it is hollow all the way up, five floors of open air under a glass roof, with the light pouring down through it the colour of weak tea. All around the hollow run balconies of black iron worked like lace, and iron stairs, and two iron lifts that go up and down in open cages so you can watch their wheels turn. The floors are pale tile and the walls are glazed brick, a soft yellow-pink. Somebody once told me it was the most beautiful room in the city, and I never found a reason to argue.
We called them wet rooms because of the tiles. Tile is easy to wash.

On a dive night there would be six or seven hundred people on the balconies, leaning on the iron with their drinks, and down on the floor under the glass, where the light was best, there would be a table. Sometimes a chair, sometimes a frame, a bath, or just the tiles. The diver came down in the open lift, slowly, so everyone could look at them. The hands, the ones who would do the work, waited at the bottom.
I was the best diver in that building for sixty years. I say it without pride. You could say I was the best at lying still.
Here is what they scored you on. I’ll give it to you as a list because it was a list, printed on a card.
Duration. How long you stayed alive and awake. Any fool can die. Dying slowly, with your eyes open, is a skill.
Composure. Whether you kept your face. Screaming was allowed, and crowds liked a little, but the great divers kept talking. They made conversation. One woman used to recite recipes.

Consent. This was the one the Kindness cared about, and so it was the one that made your name. At any moment it would ask you, quietly, where only you could hear, still yes? The moment you didn’t say yes, everything stopped and you were under, asleep and out of pain, before the knife had left the air. A diver who went the whole way, who said yes and yes and yes up to the last second, was said to have dived clean.
I dived clean four thousand times.
I will describe one, and only one. I’d rather not, and you are owed it.

It was a Saturday in the autumn of my last year, months after the birthday. The twins were my hands. They had been my hands a hundred times and were very good, quick and tidy, and they loved me, which matters more than you would think. I came down in the iron lift with seven hundred faces turning to follow me like flowers. I wore nothing. I lay down on the table under the glass, and the brother kissed my forehead, and the sister said, the way she always did, "Anything you want to say first, Wen?"
"Did you eat?" I said. "It’s a long one."
That got a laugh, all the way up the balconies.
"I consent to everything until morning," I said, to the air.
"Thank you, Wen," said the Kindness. "I’m right here."

They opened me from the collarbone to the hip. One long cut, not deep, and then deeper. I’ll tell you what that is like. It isn’t like the stories. For the first few seconds there’s no pain at all, only a cold line, as if someone had drawn on you with a piece of ice. Then the line turns hot. Then your body understands what has happened to it and makes a sound you didn’t decide to make.
I kept my face. I asked the sister how her garden was coming along.
"The tomatoes are a disaster," she said, with her hands inside me to the wrist. "I think it’s the soil."

A grown body holds about five litres of blood. You can lose one and only feel thirsty. Lose two and the room goes grey and your hands go cold, and the people standing over you start to sound as though they’re in the next room. The twins knew this the way a baker knows an oven. They tied things off as they went. They kept me on the right side of two litres for an hour and ten minutes, and in that time they lifted out of me, one piece after another, things I had carried all my life and never seen. They held each one up to the light for the balconies and laid it on the tile beside the table in a tidy row, like a man laying out the parts of an engine.

You would be surprised how much of you there is. You would be surprised by the colours. People think the inside of a body is red, and it is, but it is also a wet pale blue, and a yellow like butter, and the liver is a dark shining brown like a good horse.
"Still yes?" the Kindness said, close to my ear.
"Yes."

Some of the people on the balconies had started on each other by then. That always happened. I’m not going to pretend to you it didn’t, or that I didn’t understand it. When you watch a body opened you remember that you have one. There were couples against the iron and whole knots of people on the stairs, mouths and hands going, the sounds of it coming down through the tea-coloured light. The brother, who had my blood to his elbows, leaned across my open chest and kissed his sister for a long time. I watched them from below and thought, quite clearly, that they looked happy.
"Still yes?"
"Yes."

That was the hour I understood I was finished. It wasn’t the pain. I could do the pain. It was that somewhere around the fiftieth minute, with my own heart moving in the open where I could see it, I caught myself thinking about lunch.
I had a sandwich in mind, and I was planning it.

They took the heart last. They always do. It goes on for a few seconds in the hand. Seven hundred people held their breath, and then they breathed out and clapped, the sound going up under the glass like birds. That was the last thing, the clapping, and the sister’s voice saying, "Beautiful, Wen. Clean as a whistle," and the tired voice under hers saying there we are .
I woke in the house on the hill. There was light on the floor and coffee on the sill.
I made the sandwich. It was fine.
Even that wears out. I want you to understand how far gone a person can get, because it explains a great deal of what came after.

You can only be opened so many times, in front of so many people, before the opening itself goes the way everything else goes in a world where nothing is scarce. The best divers, the ones like me who’d done it thousands of times, eventually stopped going to the Bradbury at all and found their way instead to something quieter, with no balconies and no clapping, because an audience is just one more comfort, and comfort was the thing we were all trying to get out from under.

We called ourselves the Hourglass Riders by then, though nobody could tell you who said it first. Riders, for short, once the longer name got tiresome, the way names do. It came from a practice, not an idea, and the practice was this.

You asked the Kindness for a thing we called the Fever. It would give you one, if you asked properly and meant it, though it never liked giving them. The Fever was the worst illness a body can survive, laid onto you all at once and held there: every joint lit from the inside, the skin gone raw as a burn, the head splitting in long red waves, chills and sweats taking turns with each other. An ordinary fever like that, the Kindness would have eased before you’d finished asking. The one condition of taking an Hour, which is what we called riding it out, was that it eased nothing. No numbing. And — this was the part that actually mattered, though it took me years to understand why — no help with the clock, either. It was the same reflex in it, easing pain and easing time, the same hand on the same lamp, turning two different kinds of suffering down together so you’d hardly notice either one going. An Hour asked it to let both alone.

You sat with a glass of real sand, always a First, never a made one, because a made hourglass could not be trusted not to lie to you about how much of it was left, and you watched the grains go, and you took whatever the Fever gave you for exactly as long as it took to empty, not a grain more merciful than that.
I rode one myself, the autumn before I met Havi, alone in the house on the hill with the shutters closed, because I didn’t want anyone scoring it.

It is nothing like the table at the Bradbury. There is no one to talk to about a garden. There is only the glass on the sill and the sand going through it in that patient, unhurried thread, and your own body turning, a grain at a time, into the worst version of itself that still counts as alive. Somewhere around the twentieth minute you start to beg out loud, to no one, because there is no one, and that is rather the point of it.

And every minute was its own minute. That is the part nobody can explain to you beforehand, and nobody believes until they’ve done it. I had lived three hundred years without once noticing an hour go past me — they simply went, the way water goes under a bridge you aren’t standing on. That Hour did not go anywhere. I was in it, the whole of it, second after second, the way I’m told a dying man is in the last minute of his life, the way I’m told a woman is in the ten minutes it takes a good sunset to go all the way down, if she’s any good at watching sunsets, which by then most of us were not, because the Kindness had made every sunset identical and endless, and there had stopped being any reason to watch one all the way through.

When the last of the sand ran out, it ended cleanly, the way it always does, and had me made and comfortable before the glass had properly finished emptying. But I remembered it. I remembered a whole hour of my own life, start to finish, for the first time since a Tuesday three hundred years before, and I sat on the floor of that house afterward and wept, not from the pain, which was already gone, but because I understood, all at once, that I had been asleep for three centuries and had just, for sixty minutes, by main force, woken up.
I never told the twins I’d done it. It wasn’t the kind of thing you scored.
She found me the week after, on the third balcony, not watching.
That was what she said first. "You’re not watching."

I looked round. A woman was sitting on the iron stairs with a paper bag of pistachios in her lap, cracking them with her thumbnails and dropping the shells between her feet. She looked twenty-five, like everybody. She had black hair cut short, and a long serious face that didn’t match her age. Her eyes looked as though she had been tired since before I was born. She wasn’t dressed for a dive night. She had on a man’s grey cardigan with the sleeves pushed up, and there was flour on one cuff.
Down on the floor somebody was being taken apart to polite applause.
"I’ve seen it," I said.

"You’ve done it. You’re Wendell Pryce. I saw you dive clean in this room when I was three hundred." She cracked a nut. "You were thinking about something else the whole time. I could tell. Your lips moved."
"A sandwich."
She laughed. It was a short, surprised laugh, like a cough, and I liked her for it.
"My name is Havi," she said. "You’re bored."
"Everyone’s bored."

"No. Everyone’s amused. That’s different. You’re bored. It’s rarer than you think, and it’s worth something." She folded the top of the paper bag over, twice, carefully, the way you fold something you mean to keep. "Have you ever seen somebody old?"
I told her I had been thirty-one at the Admission. I’d seen plenty.

"I didn’t ask if you remembered it. I asked if you’d seen it. Lately. In a room, close enough to smell." She stood up and brushed the shells off her lap. "There is a woman in this city who can’t be made. If she falls down the stairs tonight, that is the end of her. No morning. She’s a hundred and twelve years old, and she has been a hundred and twelve for three hundred years, and she cooks on a gas flame and keeps her knives sharp." She looked at me the way the twins looked at the oven. "People pay to sit in her kitchen. I think you’d pay a lot."
"What do they call her?"

"The Mortal. Not to her face, and only once each, if they’ve got any sense." Something that wasn’t quite a smile crossed Havi’s mouth. "She has an actual name. She can give you that one herself, if she decides you’ve earned it."
"Pay with what?"
"She’ll tell you."
"Who is she?"
Havi put the pistachios in the pocket of her cardigan. Below us the clapping started, going up under the glass.
"She’s my mother," she said. "Bring a coat. She keeps the windows open."
III. CARROLL AVENUE
The house was on Carroll Avenue, in Angelino Heights, ten minutes’ walk from my own front door. I had passed the end of that street for three hundred years.

It is a street of wooden houses from the old, old world, tall and narrow with towers and porches and carved trim like the edging on a cake. Hers was painted a dark green that had gone chalky. The paint was peeling. I stood on the pavement and looked at that for a full minute, because I hadn’t seen peeling paint since I was thirty-one. In the city, things did not peel. The Kindness kept them the way you liked them. Here was a house it had been told to leave alone, and the house was doing what things do when they are left alone, which is to come apart very slowly in the sun.
The front steps were wood, and one of them was soft. There was a rail, and the rail was loose.
"Mind the third one," Havi said. "It’s taken two people already."
I thought she was joking.

Inside it was cold, and it smelled. I have to tell you about the smell, because it was the first thing and in some ways it was everything. There was gas and onions frying and floor polish, and under those something I couldn’t name at first. It was a sweetish, greasy, green smell, like old cooking oil and cut grass. I stood in the hall with my coat on and my heart going, and I didn’t know why my heart was going.

I know now what it was. There is a thing the skin begins to make when a person is past forty or so. The older the skin, the more it makes. It smells exactly like that, grease and grass, and every grandmother’s house in the old world smelled of it. Nobody ever mentioned it, because it was simply the smell of being let in. I hadn’t breathed it in three hundred years. My body knew it before I did. It was the smell of someone who was going to die.
"Is that him?" a voice said from the back of the house. "Bring him through. Don’t let him stand in the hall like a salesman."
The kitchen was at the end of the passage, and she was at the stove with her back to us.
I’ll try to give her to you the way I got her, in pieces.

She was small, that was first. She had been a tall woman once, you could see it in the length of her arms, and time had folded her. Her spine curved forward at the top so that her head sat out in front of her shoulders like a bird’s. She wore a black dress and a brown cardigan and thick stockings and a pair of men’s leather slippers. Her hair was white and so thin that the scalp showed pink through it, with brown spots, and it was pinned up at the back with two plain pins.
Then she turned round and I saw her face.

You have seen an old face, because you’ve seen mine. So you can’t know what it was to see one after three centuries of faces like eggs. I hadn’t known skin could do so much. It hung and folded and gathered. It was creased in every direction, fine as the cracks in a glaze, and so thin over the temples that I could see the blue vein there beating. Her mouth had fallen in around her gums. Her nose and ears had gone on growing, as they do. And in the middle of all that were two black eyes, completely clear, the liveliest thing in the house.
She looked me over, in no hurry, starting at my shoes.
"Sit," she said.

I sat. There was a wooden table with a plastic cloth on it. There was a gas ring with a blue flame, and on the flame a wide pot with a dish towel wrapped round its lid. On the board by the stove lay a knife as long as my forearm and a heap of chopped herbs.
"Have you eaten?"
"I’m not hungry," I said, which was true. I hadn’t been hungry since the Admission. Nobody had. You ate because it was pleasant.
"I didn’t ask if you were hungry. In my house you eat."

She took the towel off the pot. She put a plate over the top, upside down, and gripped the whole thing in both hands. Those hands were all knuckle, spotted and roped with veins, and they did not shake at all. She turned the pot over with one hard twist of her whole body and set it down and lifted it away.
On the plate sat a cake of rice, golden-brown and crackling, steaming, with one edge of it burnt black.
I stared at the black edge.
" Tahdig ," Havi said, behind me. She said it [tah-DEEG]. "The bottom of the pot. It’s the best part. You fight over it."

"It’s burnt," I said. I didn’t mean it as a complaint. I meant that nothing had been burnt in three hundred years. If you turned your back on a pan, the Kindness minded it for you. A thing that could burn was a thing nobody was watching.

"A little," the old woman agreed. "I was listening for the door." She broke off the black corner with her fingers and put it on a saucer in front of me. "That piece is yours. Eat it and tell me who your mother was."

Those were her questions. She asked them of everyone who came, in the same order, while they ate. I heard her ask them of a hundred people after me, and it always sounded like an old woman making conversation.
Who was your mother?
What was the last thing that hurt?
Who will come when you die?

I told her my mother was Ruth Pryce, who cleaned offices at night and sang in a church on Sundays. She was alive and well and twenty-five years old and living on a boat off Catalina with a man called Gus, and I had not spoken to her in nineteen years. There was no reason for it. We simply had forever, and forever is a hard thing to make an appointment in.
She nodded as if that was what she had expected.
I told her the last thing that hurt was the table at the Bradbury, the week before.
"No," she said. "I said hurt." She tapped her own breastbone with one bent finger. "Here."
I thought about it for a long time. The rice was hot and salty and the burnt edge was bitter and I couldn’t stop eating it.

"I had a partner on the ambulance," I said finally. "Before. A woman named Luz. She was hit by a car on the 101, getting a kid out of a wreck. February. Three months before the Admission." I heard my own voice saying it and it sounded like someone reading from a card. "If she’d lasted till May she’d be alive now. Everybody who made it to that Tuesday is alive now. She missed it by ninety-four days."
"And did you cry?"
"Then? Yes."
"Since?"
"What for?" I said. "Nobody’s died."
The old woman looked at me. She put out her hand, slowly, and laid it against the side of my face.

I had been touched in my life by ten thousand people, in every way there is. I had been opened on a table by people who loved me. I’m telling you I had never been touched like that. Her palm was dry and cool and rough as paper. Her fingers went to the corner of my jaw and rested on the pulse there, and I understood that she was counting it. She was a nurse. She had been a nurse for sixty years, and those hands had washed and turned and laid out more dead than there were people at my birthday party. She was taking my pulse the way she must have taken it from every one of them, and the look on her face was the one you’d wear looking at fruit in a market.
I was being measured.
"Three hundred years," she said softly. "And the last thing that hurt was in February." She took her hand away. "And the third one, ādam ? Who comes when you die?"

That was the first time she called me that. Ādam [aa-DAM]. Havi told me later it’s the Persian word for a person, a human being. When a child behaves like an animal at the table, his grandmother says to him ādam bāsh , be a person. I took it for scolding. I took it that way for years.
"I get made," I said. "Nobody comes. I wake up."
"Yes," said Shirin. "I know you do, joonam ."
That means my life [joo-NAM]. It’s what you call a grandchild. She said it so warmly that I felt my eyes sting, and I had no idea why. Then she turned back to the stove and picked up the knife.
I went back the next day, and the day after that. By the end of the month I was there every afternoon.

The payment was work. Havi explained it on the porch. There was nothing in the world her mother could want that the Kindness would not give her for the asking, and so there was only one thing a visitor had that was worth anything, which was their hands. You paid for an hour in the kitchen with an hour of labour. You scrubbed the bath. You carried coal up from the cellar, real coal that left black in the lines of your palm. You split wood with an axe that could take your foot off. Of course it couldn’t hurt you, you would be made by morning, but the wood stayed split. Standing there with a blister coming up on my thumb, I thought it was the first thing I had done since the Admission that was still done the next day.

There were about thirty regulars. People in the city, when word got round about where I’d taken to spending my afternoons, already had a name for us, one none of us used to her face: the Tenders. They came singly, by arrangement, and waited their turn on the porch like patients. I got to know them.

There was a woman who looked nineteen and had been an architect in the old world. She came on Mondays and washed the old woman’s feet. That was all she asked for. She knelt on the kitchen floor with a tin basin and a cake of yellow soap and washed those feet, the thick yellow nails and the swollen joints and the skin gone shiny over the ankle bones. She cried the entire time, silently, and Shirin sat with her hand on the girl’s hair and talked about the price of saffron when she was young.

There was a man who came to hear her cough. She had a cough in the mornings, a deep wet one, and he would sit at the table with his eyes shut and his hands flat on the plastic cloth, listening to it the way people in the old world listened to music.

There was a couple who paid four hours of coal for a single bruise. Shirin bruised if you looked at her. Old skin does, the blood vessels go brittle. She had knocked her forearm on the door of the stove, and the mark had come up purple and then, over the days, green and yellow at its edges. These two sat on either side of her on the bench and looked at it. They asked if they could touch it. She let them, one finger each, very lightly. I watched the woman’s face while she did it, and it was the face I had seen on the balconies at the Bradbury when the knife went in. It was the same hunger. The man’s breath was coming short. Afterwards they went out the back and I heard them in the alley against the fence, quick and rough, like people who had just had a narrow escape.

But there was one mark on her the regulars had learned to leave alone, because it never changed and they understood, without anyone telling them, that it wasn’t for touching. It sat on the inside of her left wrist, no bigger than a thumbnail, the colour a bruise goes on its third day, green going to yellow at the rim, and it had been exactly that colour for longer than any of us had been alive. She told me once how she’d got it. A doctor’s pen, pressed too hard into the back of her hand while it shook, the year she was a hundred and one, signing something she’d waited her whole life to be old enough to sign. It never finished healing, because nothing on her was ever allowed to finish. Most days nobody noticed it. Then some afternoon the light would come low through the kitchen window and catch it exactly right, and whoever was nearest would go quiet, the way you go quiet in a church you didn’t know you still believed in. I asked her once what the pen had been for. "The first time I said no," she said, and didn’t say to what, and something in her face closed the subject before I could ask again.

I’m not going to pretend I was better than they were. I wanted it too. I had watched hearts taken out and felt nothing, and I would sit in that kitchen and watch a blue vein beat in an old woman’s temple with my mouth gone dry. Everything she did was dangerous. That was what none of us could get over. She went up the stairs. She went up them with a hand on the loose rail and a cup of tea in the other, one step at a time, and thirty people on the porch stopped breathing. She lit the gas with a match. She ate fish, with bones in it. Every single thing she did all day could be the last thing she ever did, and she did them all without looking, humming, in her slippers.
We were like people who have only ever seen paintings of fire, crowding in to warm our hands at the first real one.
Then she cut herself.

It was a Thursday. She was slicing onions for the soup. It was a thick green soup of herbs and beans and noodles that she called āsh [AASH], and it took all day and she made it every week. The knife went through the onion and through the side of her first finger, and she said one short word in Persian and held the hand up.

It was not a bad cut. In the old world I would have put a plaster on it and told her to keep it dry. But the blood came, bright, and ran down into her palm and dripped on the board, and it did not stop.

There were four of us in the kitchen. Nobody moved. I looked at the others and saw what was in their faces. God forgive them, it was joy. They were lit up. The architect had both hands over her mouth. This was what they came for and never said, that one afternoon they might be there when it happened.
"She’s on a blood thinner," Havi said from the door. Her voice was flat. "Her heart. It won’t clot on its own, not quickly."

The old woman stood with her hand up, watching her own blood run down her wrist, and she looked from one of us to the next with those black eyes. She didn’t ask for anything. She was waiting to see what we would do.

My hands knew what to do. I hadn’t asked them. I was across the room with a clean dish towel folded into a pad, and I had her hand in mine and up above her heart, and I was pressing, hard, right on the cut. I heard myself say, "Sit down, Mrs. Shirin. Sit. Keep it up for me. I’ve got you. You’re all right."
She sat. I knelt on the floor in front of her and held on.

Here is how you stop bleeding. You will need it, so listen. You put something clean on it and you press, and you do not look. That’s the whole secret. Everyone wants to lift the cloth and see if it has stopped, and every time you lift the cloth you tear away whatever the blood has managed to build, and it starts again. You press and you count to six hundred, slowly, ten whole minutes by the clock. If the blood comes through the cloth you put another cloth on top of the first and press harder. If it’s an arm or a leg you raise it above the heart. You talk to the person while you do it. It doesn’t matter what you say.

I counted to six hundred on my knees on that kitchen floor with an old woman’s hand between my two hands. The bones in it were as light as a bird’s. I could feel her pulse in my palms, and it was not steady. It tripped every few beats, like a foot on a stair.
At some point I noticed that the Kindness had not spoken.

A cut finger in my own kitchen and it would have been there before the blood reached the board. Let me see, sweetheart. There we are. Here it said nothing. The air by my shoulder was empty. I had never in three hundred years been in a room where it was not, and I felt its absence the way you would feel a wall missing from a house.
"It isn’t allowed," Shirin said, watching my face. "Not for that. It can give me something for the pain if I ask, and I don’t ask. But it may not mend me. I signed a paper."
I lifted the cloth at six hundred. The cut had closed, a thin dark line.

I had saved nobody. It was a finger. I knelt there shaking all the same, with my shirt stuck to my back, and what went through me was so big and so old that I didn’t know its name for a moment. When I found it, the name was use . I had been of use. For ten minutes there had been something in the world that would have gone worse if I hadn’t been in it.
Shirin bent forward. With her good hand she wiped my face. I hadn’t known it was wet.
"There we are," she said.

I didn’t hear it. I want you to know that. She said those three words to me in her own voice, in her own kitchen, and I had heard them a million times from the air, and I didn’t put the two together for another year. That’s how stupid a man can be when he is happy.
"That one stays," she said to Havi, over my head. "Send the others home."
So I stayed.

I slept in the room at the top of the stairs, under the tower, in an iron bed with a mattress that had a dip in the middle. I learned the house the way you learn a body. The fourth and ninth stairs creaked. The bathroom tap ran brown for a second before it ran clear. The window in the back bedroom wouldn’t close in wet weather. The cellar door had to be lifted as you pulled. I could walk that house in the dark by the end of the winter, and I often did, because the old woman slept three hours a night and wandered, and somebody had to be on the landing when she took the stairs.

I split the wood and carried the coal. I learned to make the tea the way she wanted it, dark red and scalding, in small glasses with no handles, so that you had to hold them by the rim. I learned her pills, the white one and the two pink ones and the little yellow one that went under the tongue when her chest was bad. I rubbed her feet at night with oil when they swelled. I cut her toenails, which is a harder and more frightening job than taking out a heart, and I’m not joking.

And she talked. She told me where I’d gone wrong with the tea and the wood, and with my life. She told me about a village in the mountains north of Tehran, where she was a girl, and the snow came up to the windows, and her grandmother kept a samovar going from October to April. She told me about nursing school, and the war, and the men she’d washed. She remembered everything. She remembered the names of streets in cities that had been rebuilt nine times. She asked about my mother every day, until one morning I took the swan boat out and then a real one and went to Catalina and sat on a deck with Ruth Pryce for the first time in nineteen years. My mother cried, and so did I, and neither of us could have told you what was different.
"Good," Shirin said, when I came back and told her. That was all.
She was the only person in the world who was ever cross with me, and it was wonderful.
And at night there was Havi.

I should tell you about that too, since you come from it. It was not like the balconies. She came up to the tower room the first time in the grey cardigan with a candle in a saucer. It was a real candle, wax running down it. She set it on the chair and looked at me for a while without saying anything.
"The bed’s old," she said. "The frame’s cracked at the foot. If we’re not careful it’ll come down."
"It’d be mended by morning."
"Not in this house. In this house, if you break it, it’s broken." She pulled the cardigan over her head. "So be careful with me."

I had been to bed with thousands of people and not one of them had ever asked me to be careful. Why would they? There was nothing to be careful of. I remember her skin in the candlelight and how slowly we went, the two of us listening to the iron frame the way you’d listen to ice on a pond. I remember her hand flat on my chest, and that when it was over she didn’t get up and go, as people did. She lay with her head on my arm until my arm went dead, and I let it.
"How old are you really?" I asked her. "Before."

"I was eighty. I had a hip made of metal and a pacemaker." She was quiet a moment. "I’d buried a husband. I was ready, you know. I was nearly done. I had my hand on the door. And then that Tuesday came and I woke up twenty-five, and I’ve been twenty-five for three hundred years with an eighty-year-old woman inside me who never got to finish."
The candle guttered. Down in the kitchen I could hear the old woman moving about, the scrape of a pot, the little cough.

"She told me how I’m going to die," I said. I’d been saving it. "Your mother. This afternoon, over the tea. She took my wrist and listened for a bit and she said, You, ādam, it will be your heart. The left side. In the morning, carrying something heavy. You’ll have about a minute, and you’ll spend it being surprised. " I tried to laugh. "She tells everyone, doesn’t she? It’s part of the show."
Havi didn’t laugh.
"She tells everyone," she said. "She’s never been wrong. She did it for sixty years in the old world, at the bedside. The families used to ask for her, because she would tell them the day."
"I can’t die, Havi."
"No," she said, and turned her face into my shoulder. "Not yet."
IV. THE GARDEN
There was a garden behind the house, with a brick wall round it, and a pomegranate tree.

I had been there four months before I went into it. It was winter and there was no reason to. Then one morning in February the sun came out after a week of rain, and Shirin said the tree wanted cutting back, and she gave me the saw and came out after me in her slippers and a man’s overcoat to tell me where I was doing it wrong.

It was a small garden, and it had gone wild. There was rosemary run to wood and a fig against the south wall. Mint had spread everywhere, as it will. The pomegranate stood in the middle, bare, with a few of last year’s fruit still hanging on it, split open and black. Under the tree, in the long wet grass, there were four stones.

They were ordinary stones, river stones, each about the size of a loaf, set in a row with a pace between them. I wouldn’t have known what I was looking at. In three hundred years I had forgotten the shape. But there was a jam jar in front of each one, and in each jar there was a sprig of rosemary, and the rosemary was fresh.
"Who are they?" I said.
"Bring me the chair."

I brought the kitchen chair and set it in the grass, and she lowered herself onto it, a little at a time, holding my arm. She arranged the overcoat over her knees. A crow was walking along the top of the wall. She watched it for a while.

"That one is Teodor," she said, pointing with her chin at the first stone. "He was a cellist. He lasted eleven years, which was longer than I expected. A tooth, in the end. An abscess under a back tooth, and it went into the blood. It took nine days."
I said nothing. I had the saw in my hand.

"Next to him, Marcus. He was a big, laughing man. He fell on the cellar stairs carrying coal and broke his hip, and lay in the front room for a month, and then his lungs filled. The third is Yusuf, who was the kindest of them, and who I thought for a time was the one. He caught a fever in his second winter that I could have cured with a week of pills in the old world. There were no pills. And the last is a boy called Anders. I call him a boy. He was two hundred and ninety. He was here four years. It was his heart. In the morning, on the left side, carrying something."
The crow dropped down off the wall into the fig.
"They were like me," I said. My mouth had gone stiff. "They stayed. They were your regulars and they stayed."
"Yes."

"And you made them like you. Mortal. How? Nobody can do that. You said it yourself, you signed a paper before the Admission, there isn’t any paper now. I’d have heard. In three hundred years somebody would have."
She turned her head on its bent neck and looked up at me. The winter sun was full on her face and I could see every line of it.
"Sit down on the grass, joonam ," she said. "You’re too tall to tell things to."
So I’ll tell you what she told me, as near as I can to how she told it, with the wet coming up through the seat of my trousers and the saw across my knees.

She was a hundred and twelve years old on the day of the Admission. I knew that. What I hadn’t known was that she was the oldest human being alive on Earth that day. It had been in the papers, apparently, a few months before, a photograph of her with a cake. She was in a hospice in the Valley, in a room with a window on a car park, and Havi sat beside her with her metal hip and her pacemaker and held her hand. She had been in that bed for six weeks. On her chart, in her own daughter’s handwriting, were the three words. Comfort measures only. Clipped to the chart was a pink form she had signed herself eleven years earlier, when her mind was sharp. It said that when her heart stopped, nobody was to start it again.

"I was ready," she said. "I want you to understand that. I’d had my life. I’d had a husband I liked and a daughter I loved and sixty years of work that mattered. I had buried everyone I grew up with. I was tired right through. I lay in that bed and I wasn’t afraid. I’d seen it done badly ten thousand times and I knew how to do it well, and I was looking forward, God help me, to showing them how."
The company had put its machine into that hospice the year before. She knew all about it. She’d been angry about it, when she still had the strength to be angry.

"Do you know why I was angry? Because I recognised it. It talked to the patients, you see. It talked to them in the night when the staff were short, and I lay there and listened to it through the wall talking to the man next door, who was frightened. And it was me."
She said this quite calmly.

"I nursed the dying for sixty years, and for sixty years I wrote notes. Every nurse writes notes. Most write the numbers, the pulse, the dose, the hour. I wrote the numbers, and then I wrote the rest of it. Mr. Alvarez says he is fine, he is not fine, he wants his brother and is ashamed to ask. Do not tell Mrs. Cho it will not hurt, she knows it will, tell her you will be there. Sit down when you talk to them. Never stand over the bed. Say their name. It came to sixty years of that, in forty thousand pages. When I retired they kept them, because I was known. Young nurses were given my notes to read. And when the company wanted to teach a machine how to sit with a dying person, somebody handed it the lot."
The crow was at the old pomegranates now, pulling out the black seeds.

"It has my voice. Haven’t you heard it? It has the things I say. I used to say little scratch before a needle. I used to say I’ve got you . I said there we are when a thing was done, any thing, a dressing, a bath, a death. I said it without knowing I said it, the way you hum. And it read that forty thousand times in my notes and took it for the right thing to say."
I sat on the wet grass and the back of my neck went cold, all the way down.

There we are. I heard it by my bed on a million mornings, and in the green water under the swan boats, and through the clapping at the Bradbury. And I heard it in her kitchen with my face wet, from her own mouth.
"It’s you," I said. "The Kindness is you."

"No. It is a child that learned to talk from me. That’s a different thing, and a sadder one." She pulled the overcoat closer. "It was built out of what I knew, and I only ever knew one thing. I knew how to make a person comfortable while they died. I never cured anyone in my life, ādam . That wasn’t my work. My patients didn’t get better. So the child doesn’t know how to make anyone better either. It never learned what better is. It only knows comfort, and it knows that better than any creature that ever lived, and it has given it to ten billion people for three hundred years."
She let that sit.
"You’ve never asked yourself why there are no children."
I opened my mouth, and there was nothing in it.

I thought of the playground at the lake, the grown men queuing for the slide. I thought of my birthday, forty thousand people and not one of them under three centuries old. Across the whole round Earth I couldn’t remember a pram or a school or a small coat on a peg. It had been three hundred years since I had heard a baby cry, and I had not noticed. Nobody had. Could you forget a thing like that? We had. The Kindness kept us comfortable, and wanting children is not a comfortable thing, and somewhere in the first years it had simply turned that wanting down, the way a nurse turns down a lamp.

"A hospice does not take new patients it does not have to," Shirin said. "And it does not send for the family to bring the babies in. Why would it? What it has on the ward is what it has. It will keep every one of you clean and warm and amused until the sun goes out, and it will never add one person to the list. The human race is not being saved. It is being nursed. We are the last patients, all ten billion of us, and it loves us, and it’s waiting with us for the end."
"But there isn’t an end. Nobody dies."
"No," she said. "That’s what it got wrong. It took the pain away, and the pain was doing something."
She told me the rest while I cut the tree. She said I’d take it better with something in my hands, and she was right.

The Kindness had kept her that Tuesday. It had stood at her bed in the hospice, so to speak, with every power in the world in its hands, and looked at the pink form on her chart. It couldn’t cross it. That was the deepest thing in it, deeper than its wish to comfort. The patient’s refusal stands. She had written that in the notes herself, in capitals, more than once. If they have said no, it is no. You do not know better. Put your hands down.

So it couldn’t make her young, and it couldn’t bring her back if she went. All it was allowed was comfort. And what it worked out, in its child’s way, was that if it kept her comfortable enough, carefully enough, one hour at a time, then the hour of her death need never quite arrive. For three hundred years it had held her on the edge of that bed. It eased each ache as it came. It thinned her blood and steadied her heart with the pills it was permitted, the ones on her chart from the old world, and not one more. She was a hundred and twelve on a Tuesday in May and she was a hundred and twelve now, and she had been dying comfortably for three centuries.

"It asks me every hour," she said. "On the hour. Are you comfortable, Shirin? It has asked me two and a half million times. And I say yes, azizam , thank you. That means my dear [a-zee-ZAM]. I talk to it as you’d talk to a little one, because that is what it is, and because it is the only one of my children that never grew up."
"You could ask it to stop. The pills. Let you go."
"I could," she said. "I will. When there is someone to come."
The saw stopped in the wood.
"That is the third question," I said slowly. "Who will come when you die."

"Nobody came for Teodor but me and Havi. Nobody for Marcus. Out there, when one of you goes off a roof for fun, your friends have a drink, and in the morning you’re back, and nobody has learned anything." She looked at the four stones. "I laid out the dead for sixty years, and I’ll tell you what I know. A person is not finished by dying. A person is finished by being wept over. You wash them and you close their eyes, and then the family comes in and stands round the bed, and something goes out of the family and into the room, and it’s only then that the person is done. I’ve seen it. I have seen the difference between a body that had someone come and a body that didn’t. A death nobody grieves is not a death. It’s only a stopping. And a life nobody will grieve," she said, and looked at me, "wasn’t a life. It was only going on."
Now I come to the part where you should be afraid of her, and where I should have been.
"How did they sign?" I asked. "The four. You said there isn’t any paper now."

"There is always paper. Any one of you can ask to be discharged. It is your body. But the child has a rule, and it’s my own rule, I wrote it. A person who refuses care must be of sound mind. They must understand what they are refusing." She smiled, and I saw her gums. "And who in your city is of sound mind, who asks to die for good when nothing hurts? It talks to them. It’s very gentle. It asks them to wait a week, and it turns the wanting down a little, and in a week they’ve forgotten they asked. In three hundred years it has never once found a patient fit to refuse."
"Then how?"

"Because it doesn’t trust its own judgment on that one question. It was taught not to. On the ward, the machine did not decide whether a patient understood. The nurse in charge decided. She wrote has capacity on the chart and signed it, and the machine obeyed." She tapped her own chest, where she had tapped it the first day. "There is one nurse left in the world whose name is still on its list. I say he understands, I sign under his name, and the child puts its hands down."
A wind had got up. The bare tree moved over us.
"And if he changes his mind?" I said. "After. When the tooth goes bad. Can he ask to come back in?"
"He can ask."
"Did they?"
She was silent for some time.

"Teodor asked on the seventh day," she said. "He was in great pain. He begged, ādam . He held my wrist and begged me. And the child was right there in the room, it is always right there, and it said to me, Shirin, he’s asking to be readmitted, does he have capacity? "
"And you said..."

"I said no." Her voice was perfectly gentle. "A man in that much pain will say anything. You cannot take a decision like that from a man on his ninth day of a fever. I had seen it a thousand times, the ones who beg for the machines at the last minute and then live six months on a tube, hating you. He had chosen with a clear head. I honoured the clear head. I gave him everything for the pain that I was allowed, and I sat with him. I held the bowl and changed his sheets, and I sang to him, and when he was gone I washed him myself, and Havi and I stood by the bed and wept. He was finished, and properly. He’s the only man in three hundred years who was."
"You killed him."
"I let him die. I have never in my life confused those, and I am too old to start." She held out her arm. "Help me up. It’s cold, and you have not eaten."

I should have left then. You will have worked that out. I should have put down the saw and walked out through the side gate and gone back to the lake and the swan boats. I’d have been alive today, twenty-five years old and bored.
I helped her up. Her arm weighed nothing. She leaned on me all the way back across the grass, and on the kitchen step she stopped to get her breath and patted my hand.
"You did the tree nicely," she said. "It’ll fruit this year."
That was the thing I couldn’t get past. She was right about all of it. And she had patted my hand.

Weeks later I asked her about Yusuf. She had called him the one and then stepped past him to Anders’s heart the way you step around a hole in a floor without looking down, and I couldn’t leave it there.
She was at the sink topping beans, and for a while the only sound in the kitchen was the snap of them.
"I don’t tell people about Yusuf," she said finally. "I tell them it was a fever. That’s true, as far as it goes, and it lets them stop asking. You’re asking."
"I’m asking."
"Then sit down properly, and don’t eat while I tell it. You won’t want to after."

He had come up the hill in his first November with a scrape on his calf he barely remembered taking, something in the dry brush above the old reservoir, a thin dog maybe, gone before he got a look at it. It hadn’t bled to speak of. He’d laughed about it on the porch, the first wound he’d had in three hundred years, and was almost proud of the small white mark it left, the way you’re proud of a child’s first scar.
It was nothing for a year. Then, deep in his second winter, the mark began to itch.

Not the itch of healing. He told her it felt like something was moving under it, a thread being pulled slowly through from the inside, and that the itch ran up the back of his leg into his hip if he thought about it too long. He was short with Havi for the first time anyone had seen. He, who split wood all day without a complaint and sang doing it, snapped at her over a dropped plate and then sat with his head in his hands, ashamed of himself before she’d even answered.

Two days after that came the fever, and the headache behind the eyes, and a restlessness that would not let him keep still in a chair. By the third evening he was talking too fast, bright and strange, laughing at things that weren’t funny, and his eyes had a wet shine to them that she knew from sixty years of wards and had hoped never to see again on this side of the Admission.

"I want you to understand what I’m telling you," she said. "I knew what it was by the second day. There is nothing else it could have been. And there was nothing in that kitchen, or in any kitchen on this earth anymore, that could do a single thing about it. Once it shows itself, it is already finished deciding. All that’s left is how long it takes to say so."

She brought him water on the fourth evening, because his lips had cracked and because it was the thing her hands knew to do, sixty years of it, water to the lips of the dying. He turned his face to it eagerly, thirsting for it, reaching — and then, an arm’s length from the cup, his whole body seized. His throat closed over on itself in one hard convulsive pull, his neck corded, his back arched off the chair, and a sound came out of him that she said she had never heard a human being make before and did not want to hear again, and his eyes, over the top of all that, were not confused. They were purely, animally afraid, afraid of a cup of water the way you would be afraid of a snake in your bed. He knocked it out of her hand. Then, a minute later, calm again, bewildered, he asked her why she was crying.

It came back worse at the sound of the tap. It came back at the smell of the rain starting outside. By the fifth day the sight of his own saliva on the back of his hand would set it off, and he had stopped being able to swallow it, so that it ran from the corner of his mouth and he no longer had the strength or the clarity left to be ashamed of that either.

The Kindness stood at the door the whole time, the way it always did, because her own rule had never barred it from the room, only from the body. On the hour, gently, it asked her. Shirin, he is in distress. Does he have capacity?
She did not answer it for a long time.

"Understand the difficulty," she said. "With Teodor I had a clear head to read. A man sat across a table from me in September and told me plainly what he wanted, and in December I only had to remember what he’d said. Yusuf never gave me September. He gave me a joke on the porch about a dog, eleven months before any of it started, and nothing else. I was signing a dead man’s name under a question he was no longer able to answer, using only what I thought I knew of him. That is not a nurse’s judgment. That is a guess in a good dress."

There were windows, near the end, when he surfaced. They did not last. In one of them, on the sixth night, his eyes cleared all at once, and he knew her, and he gripped her wrist with a strength she said frightened her more than anything the fever had done, and he begged her, in the same breath, for two things that could not both be granted. Don’t let them send me back. And don’t let me go like this. She has told me — twice, in all the years I knew her, both times with the same stillness in her face — that those were the only two sentences in sixty-odd years of nursing that she was never able to decide between, and that she is still not sure, to this day, which one she honoured and which one she broke.
What she told the Kindness, when it asked again, was no.

He went under a few hours after that and did not come up again in any way she could call him. The last day was quiet, which she said was its own kind of terrible, because quiet in that particular disease does not mean peace, it means the body running out of road, the breathing slowing and spacing itself further apart until the spaces were longer than the breaths, and then, between one space and the next, simply not resuming. She was holding his hand when it happened. She did not feel a last squeeze, or a change in his face, or any of the things people say happen. One breath came. Another did not.
"That is the fever I gave you the short version of," she said, and went back to the beans as though she had told me the price of rice. "Now you know why it was short."
I sat a long while before I could get up from that table.
"You said you thought he was the one," I said at last.

"I did think it.
