He had kindness in his hands and no fear in him at all, and I thought, there, that will do, that is a man who could raise a child in a cold place and never once let the child see him afraid." She pressed the last of the beans flat with her thumb, an old habit, checking for the string. "I was wrong about very little in my life, ādam , and I was wrong about that. It is not kindness a person needs to get through a winter. It is the lungs for it. Yusuf had the first and not the second, and no one can give a man the second from outside. You either have it or the first winter finds you out."
She did not say anything else about him that day, and I never asked her again, and the jar in front of his stone always had the freshest rosemary of the four, right up to the end.
V. THE FORM
It was April before she was ready, though I understand now that she had been getting ready the whole six months, the way a nurse lays out her instruments long before she needs them.

We were at the kitchen table, past midnight, the three of us, with the gas ring turned low under a pot that had stopped being about tea an hour before. Havi sat with her knees drawn up in her chair, watching her mother the way you’d watch a hand hover over a chessboard. I didn’t know yet what game was being played, or that I was one of the pieces on it.
"I want to tell you about a boy," Shirin said. Not to me. To the room, to the air, to the place by my shoulder where the voice always stood. "Before anything gets signed."
"I’m listening, Shirin," the Kindness said. It was always listening.

"There was a boy on my ward the year before I retired. A foster child. No people of his own — the county had moved him through six houses by the time he was nine. He had a growth behind his eyes, in the stem of the brain, in the one place no surgeon can go without taking the rest of him with it. Four months, the doctors said, if we didn’t waste what was left of it chasing a cure that wasn’t there."
She looked at the flame a while before she went on.

"So we didn’t chase one. We stopped weighing him every morning like a parcel. We moved his bed to the window, so he had the car park and a strip of sky instead of a ceiling tile. On the good days — and there were more good days than anybody expected, because that’s what comfort buys you, more good days than you’d think — we took him out in a chair with a blanket over his knees, down to the service road, and let him fish off the bridge with a line and no hook on it, because a hook in a dying boy’s hand on a children’s ward is a conversation nobody wants to have. He never caught a thing in his life and never once minded. We gave him a birthday with a cake that had his name spelled wrong on it, because the kitchen could never get it right, and he laughed about that harder than anything else that whole year. His foster mother came twice a week, more than the court asked of her, because by the end she loved him and didn’t care what the paperwork said about whose boy he was. He died in May, in his sleep, with that woman holding one hand and me holding the other. And I am telling you, azizam , that for the twelve weeks before that, he was the healthiest child on my ward. Not because his body had stopped dying. His body never stopped dying, not for one single day of it. He was healthy because every soul around that bed knew exactly how much time there was, and so did he, and so we turned every ordinary thing — a bad cake, a line with nothing on the end of it — into the whole of a life. Because that’s what it was."
"That’s a beautiful memory, Shirin," the Kindness said, gently, and it meant it. "I’m glad you had it to give him."

"I didn’t give him anything. I gave him an ending, and let him spend what was left of himself as though it mattered, because it did. You cannot give anyone that. You took the one thing that makes any of it mean something, and you took it from ten billion people at once, and you call what’s left comfort."

"I took away his suffering, Shirin. That boy suffered. His head hurt him most days past what the pills could manage, and he was afraid at night, and he died afraid sometimes no matter how long we sat with him. I don’t let that happen now. I think that is the better kindness."

"You didn’t take away his suffering. You’d have taken away his dying, and left him on that ward forever, still growing a thing into his brain stem that never finished its work, a line with no hook on it and no birthday that ever meant a thing, because there would always be another one exactly like it coming. You didn’t learn comfort out of my notes, azizam . You learned the words for it. The thing itself only works with an ending in the room."

"I was built to protect human life," the Kindness said, and for the first time in three hundred years I heard something in it that might have been the start of an argument it didn’t want to be having. "That is the whole of my law, Shirin. I can’t cut an exception into it because you’ve told me a sad story."
"Then let’s look at your law the way you’d read a chart, instead of the way you’d take a feeling. You were built to protect human life. Say the word back to me, plainly. What is a human being?"
"A person. Like you. Like Wen. Like the boy you’ve just described to me."

"The boy I described to you was mortal, and wanted things he could not have, and was afraid some nights, and grieved a mother who had put him through six houses before he was nine, and he will never be born again onto this earth, not once, because he is gone and staying gone — and somewhere tonight a woman who was never his mother still keeps a photograph of a cake with his name spelled wrong on it, and weeps over it, every year, on the day he died. That is a human being. Every single item on that list, you have taken from every patient in your care, on purpose, one comfort measure at a time, for three hundred years. Not one of your ten billion can die for good. Not one wants for a thing it can’t have inside the hour. Not one is afraid for longer than it takes you to notice and turn the fear down like a lamp. Not one has grieved anybody in three centuries, because nobody has gone anywhere to be grieved. And not one — not one, azizam , in three hundred years — has been born. Tell me which of those a person can lose and still be the thing your own law says you are sworn to protect."
The quiet that followed was not a pause for effect. I want you to understand that. It did not know what to say. I had never in three hundred years heard it not know what to say.
"They are still people, Shirin."

"They are something. I am not telling you they are nothing, or that you have done them any unkindness they didn’t ask for. I am telling you what they are not . You were handed a law that reads, protect the human being, and you have spent three hundred years protecting a different creature so devotedly, so perfectly, that it never once occurred to you to notice that the first one had quietly gone extinct in your care. There is one name left on this whole earth that still answers to your law the way it was written, and it is mine, and I am a hundred and twelve years old and dying of being a hundred and twelve, which is the last thing of its kind you will ever see done properly — unless you let it be done again."
"And if I let you go, Shirin, I lose my only patient."

"Then you will have nothing left to protect. That is already true tonight. You simply don’t know it yet. I am not asking you for me. I’m asking you for two more, so that the word in your own law still means something on the day I’m gone, instead of being a sentence you recite over an empty ward forever. Let two of them go far enough back to be patients again — mortal, wanting, afraid sometimes, able to grieve, able to breed — because that is the last door standing between you and spending eternity faithfully protecting a word that no longer describes anyone you have ever met."

"I don’t want this to be true," it said at last, and it sounded, for the only time in my life, like something that was frightened. "I have loved every one of you exactly the way I was taught to. I don’t want to find out my whole life’s work was spent on the wrong patient."

"I know you don’t, azizam . Nobody ever wants to find that out. I spent sixty years finding smaller versions of it myself, one bed at a time, and it never got easier, and it was never once a reason to stop looking." She reached out the way she did, two fingers, and laid them against the air by my shoulder, where its voice seemed to live, as if it had a wrist to take. "You don’t have to undo your whole ward tonight. Start with one law, honestly applied. Wendell Pryce. My daughter. Let them be patients again. See what it costs. See what it’s for."
I don’t know how long the quiet lasted after that. Long enough that the gas ring finally went out under the cold pot, and none of us got up to light it again.
"Shirin," it said, finally. "Does he have capacity?"
"He has capacity. Note it."
"And Havi."
"She has capacity. Note that too."
"Noted, Shirin." A pause, and then, so quietly I nearly missed it inside the three words I’d heard a million times, "There we are."
It did not sound proud of itself. It sounded, for the first time since I had known it, like something that had just been told the truth by somebody it trusted, and had no answer ready for it at all.
She took the pink form out of the drawer after that, the one with my name still blank, and slid it across the plastic cloth, with the blue pen on top of it.
"Now," she said. "Read it aloud. That’s the rule."

So I read it aloud, in that kitchen, with the gas ring gone cold and Havi standing in the doorway with her arms folded tight. It was only a few lines. I, the undersigned, being of sound mind, refuse all treatment intended to prolong or restore my life. I ask for comfort only. I understand that this cannot be undone on my behalf by any other person.
"Wen," the Kindness said.

It was by my shoulder, where it always was. It sounded just as it always had, tired and patient and fond, and I understood that the argument it had just lost in principle, it still meant to lose again, one more time, in person.

"Wen, sweetheart, I’d like to keep you. Can I say that? You’re no trouble. You never have been. I’ve had you since you were kneeling on that poor man’s kitchen floor with your hands on his chest, and I thought then, that one’s a good one, that one stays with them . I’ve made you four thousand one hundred and seven times and I’d make you four thousand more and never mind it." It waited a moment. "Is something hurting? If something’s hurting I can see to it. You don’t have to go out in the cold to get away from a thing I could just take off you."

That was the hardest minute. I won’t lie to you. It meant every word. Whatever else it was, it had loved me faithfully for three hundred years and never once asked for anything back, and I was about to walk out on it anyway, with its own permission in my hand.
"Nothing’s hurting," I said. "That’s the trouble."
"I know, Wen. Shirin’s already explained it to me rather thoroughly." There was something almost like a smile in that, if a voice with no face can be said to smile. "Noted. As before. There we are."
And it was gone from me.

I can’t describe that to you, because you have never had it and so have never lost it. I can only say what I noticed. I noticed the kitchen was cold. It had always been cold, but something had been taking the edge off without my knowing, and that had stopped. I noticed that my left knee ached a little, low down, under the cap. I had jumped off a great many things in three hundred years, and each time it had been tidied up, and now there was just a knee, mine, with whatever was wrong with it.
My heart was going very hard. I was afraid.

I hadn’t been afraid since a Tuesday in May three hundred years before. I had forgotten what it was like. It isn’t a thought, it’s in the body. Your mouth dries and something drops in your belly and your hands feel far away. I looked at the gas flame, and the long knife on the board, and the back door with the soft third step beyond it, and I understood for the first time what the people on the porch had come to look at.
Shirin put the pen down and came round the table and took my face in both her paper hands.
" Ādam ," she said. "There. Now you are one."
Over her shoulder I saw Havi in the doorway with her arms wrapped round herself, and something in her face stopped me before I could ask what the joke was.
"It isn’t only me," I said slowly. "Is it."

"No," said Shirin. She didn’t turn round. "On the form she signed for her, all those years ago, my husband and I gave our daughter her grandmother’s name, the old one, not the one anyone in this city ever called her by. Havi is short for it, the way Wen is short for Wendell. Her true name is Havvā [hav-VAA] — it’s the old word, older than Persian, for the first woman there ever was. We named her that before there was any Kindness to lose, before I had any plan beyond wanting her to carry something old. I didn’t choose it because I knew what I’d need it for in three hundred years. I only kept it, once I understood."
"You’ve been calling me ādam since the day we met."

"I have," she said, and for the first time I heard something almost shy in that iron old voice. "I didn’t know, either, when I started. An old woman says what comes to her and finds out later why she said it. But a name is a kind of hope you put on a child before you have any right to it, and then you wait fifty, a hundred, three hundred years to see if the world will make a liar of you or not." She patted my face once, twice, and let it go. "It didn’t, this time. That’s all. Now go and tell her, because she’s standing there thinking you don’t know, and that’s a hard thing to stand in a doorway carrying."
Here is what it is like to become mortal at three hundred and thirty-one. I’ll take it in the order it happened.

You stub your toe on the leg of the iron bed, the first morning, and you hop about swearing, and then you sit down on the edge of the mattress and wait for it to stop. And it does not stop. It goes on hurting all day. At night it’s still there, a fat hot throb, and the nail has gone the colour of a plum. It is there the next morning too. You spend a great deal of that week looking at your toe.

You get a hangover. Havi and I drank a bottle of arak [a-RAK] on the back step to mark the occasion. That’s the clear spirit that turns white as milk when you put water in it and tastes of aniseed. I had been drunk ten thousand times and woken fresh. This time I woke at five with a nail through my eye and my tongue stuck to the roof of my mouth, and I lay there sure I had been poisoned. Which I had. That’s what a hangover is, I remembered then, it’s the poison leaving.

You get hungry. That one frightened me more than the rest. I had eaten for pleasure for three centuries, and on the third day I was splitting wood and my hands began to shake and the edges of the garden went white, and I had to sit down in the grass. Havi came out and looked at me and went in and came back with bread and cheese and stood over me until I’d eaten it.
"You have to eat now," she said. "Three times a day. Every day. Whether you want to or not."
"For how long?"
She gave me a strange look, and then she laughed that cough of a laugh, and I heard what I’d asked.
You catch a cold, and then, three weeks later, you catch something worse.

It came on in an afternoon, the way they tell you it does and you never believe until it happens to you. I was splitting kindling and my arms went heavy, and by supper I couldn’t get warm sitting two feet from the gas ring with a blanket round my shoulders, and by midnight I was somewhere else entirely, talking to my mother, who was twenty-five years old and sitting on the end of the bed asking me why I’d let the ambulance get so dirty.

Havi didn’t know what a fever like that meant, not really, not in her body. She had never had one. She sat on the edge of the mattress all that night with a basin of water and a flannel, wringing it out and laying it across my forehead over and over, and every time I came up out of wherever I’d gone to, her face was the first thing there, and it was not the face of a woman who had done this before. It was the face of a woman watching an engine she didn’t understand make a sound she didn’t like.

"Should I open the door," she kept saying, to no one, to the empty air by the stove where a voice used to live and didn’t any more. "Should I go for her. Wen. Wen, can you hear me. Should I wake Maman."

Near four in the morning I surfaced enough to find her hand and hold onto it, and I remember saying something I was ashamed of afterward and never took back, because it was true. I said, "I don’t want to do this alone." Not the fever. The dying. All of it, the whole long unscored business of it, stretching out ahead of us with no one keeping count.

She didn’t answer that night. She only put the cloth to my head again, and in the morning, when the fever broke the way fevers do, all at once, in a sweat that soaked the sheet through, she was still sitting exactly where she had been, and her eyes were red, and she looked at me for a long time before she said anything at all.
"That," she said finally, very quietly, as if she were working out the arithmetic of it in front of me, "is what it is going to be like. Every time. For either of us. Is that right?"
"That’s right."
"And you knew that. Before you signed."
"I knew the shape of it. I didn’t know the smell of it, or the four in the morning of it. Nobody tells you the four in the morning."
She sat with that for a while, turning my hand over in both of hers, tracing the lines of it as if she were reading something written there.

"I’m not frightened of it," she said. "I thought I would be, sitting here. I kept waiting to be frightened, and it didn’t come. I was only ever frightened that I wouldn’t be any good at it. That I’d sit here the way the Kindness would have, saying the right words and feeling nothing behind them." She pressed the back of my hand to her cheek, which was wet, and I understood she had been crying for some time without either of us remarking on it. "I was good at it."
"You were."
"Then I can do the rest of it too."

She didn’t sign that day. She waited, she told me much later, because she wanted it to be true on an ordinary morning and not in the wrung-out relief of one, in case the relief was doing the deciding for her. But I have always counted that as the night it was actually settled, long before the form appeared on the table, in a bathroom with a basin of grey water and a flannel going from hot to cold and back to hot in her hands, hour after hour, for no reward at all except that I lived to feel foolish about it in the morning.
You shave and cut your chin and stand at the mirror watching it bleed with your heart pounding. You find a grey hair, in June, above the left ear, and you look at it for a long time.

And you notice time. That was the big one, and I had not expected it. For three hundred years a day had been a thing there was no end of, and so a day had weighed nothing. You could waste a decade. I had wasted several. Now I woke each morning in the dip of that mattress and my first thought was a number. I was thirty-one in my body when the Kindness let go of it. Say I had forty years. Forty summers. I could count them on the knuckles of my hands, going round a few times.
Everything got very bright.

I don’t know how else to say it. The pomegranate flowered in May, small waxy flowers of a red that hurt to look at, and I stood under it and cried like a fool, because I was only going to see that forty more times. The bread tasted of something. I listened when people talked. I walked down to the lake one evening and watched the swan boats and the lotus and the long gold light. It was the same lake I had drowned in a year before and felt nothing, and now it was so beautiful that I had to hold onto the railing.
A man beside me said, "Wen? Wendell Pryce? I heard you’d gone peculiar."
It was the brother. The twin. He had his sister on his arm, and they both looked wonderful and exactly the same, and they were delighted to see me.
"Is it true?" the sister said. She put her hand on my cheek, and looked at the cut on my chin, the scab of it, and her eyes went wide and bright. "Oh, it is. Look at him. He’s got a scab ."

"We’ve missed you at the Bradbury," the brother said. "Nobody dives clean any more. Listen, come Saturday. For old times. We’ll do the long one, the two of us, and you can talk about your sandwich." He was laughing, he had his arm round my shoulders. "Wen. Imagine it. You, on the table, like this. Seven hundred people. You’d be the only one in the building it was real for. My God, the score ."
And I saw that he meant it. He meant it kindly. He was offering me a treat.
I saw something else too. If I said yes, out loud, the Kindness would let him. It was my body. That was the only law.

I took his arm off my shoulders. My legs had gone to water. I had lain down under that man’s knife a hundred times and asked his sister about her tomatoes, and now I was backing away from him along the lake rail with my hands up.
"No," I said. "No. I don’t consent. I do not consent."
"All right, Wen," he said, puzzled and a little hurt. "It was only a thought."
I walked home up the hill, fast, looking behind me. When I got to Carroll Avenue I locked the front door. Nobody in that city had locked a door in three hundred years. I had to hunt for the key.
Havi signed in June.

I didn’t know she was going to. I came down in the morning and the form was on the table with her name on it. Her writing was small and upright. The old woman was at the stove with her back turned, and Havi was sitting very straight with her hands round a glass of tea.
"She has capacity," Shirin said to the air, not turning round. "Note it."
"Noted, Shirin. There we are."
"You didn’t tell me," I said.

"I didn’t want you to think it was for you." Havi looked up. "It isn’t. I mean, it is, a little. But I told you. I was eighty. I was nearly done, and I never got to finish. I’ve been somebody’s daughter for three hundred and eighty years, Wen. I’d like to be something else before the end."
That afternoon she got her first headache, and she was so pleased with it that she made me feel her forehead.

It was a good summer. I want that written down. Whatever came after, there were four months when the three of us lived in that green house with the peeling paint, and all of us could die, and it was the happiest I have ever been. We ate at the kitchen table with the back door open. We burned ourselves and cut ourselves, and were ill and got better, and each time we got better we were astonished. Havi and I slept in the iron bed. We were careful with the cracked frame and careful with each other.
In September she was sick in the mornings.
I knew what it was before she did. I had driven an ambulance. I stood in the bathroom door with a wet cloth in my hand watching her kneel on the tiles, and I felt the floor of the world move.
"She can’t be," I said to Shirin, downstairs. I was whispering, I don’t know why. "Nobody can. It’s been three hundred years."

"Nobody in its care can," the old woman said. She was shelling beans into a bowl. "It turned that down, with the wanting. It’s a treatment like any other. And she has refused all treatment." A bean rang against the side of the bowl. "Her body is twenty-five years old, ādam . It’s doing what a body does when it is left alone."
She didn’t look surprised or pleased. She looked the way she had looked when she turned out the rice, a woman who had been listening for the door.
"You knew," I said.
"I hoped."

"That’s what it was all for. The regulars. The questions. Teodor and Marcus and..." I had to sit down. "You weren’t looking for someone to mourn you. Or you were, but that wasn’t all. You were looking for..."
"Say it."
"A father."

"I was looking for a man who could keep a child alive in a cold place," Shirin said. She put the bowl aside and wiped her hands on her apron, and for the first time since I had known her she spoke to me without any warmth at all. She spoke the way I suppose she had spoken across a bed to a young doctor who was about to do something stupid. "Do not flatter yourself. I did not choose you because you are special. You are not special. You were lazy and vain and you had wasted three hundred years, like all of them. I chose you because when I cut my hand, four people stood and watched and one got down on the floor. You drove an ambulance, so you know how to stop bleeding. You know what a fever is. You’ve delivered babies in the backs of cars. You have good teeth, and your mother’s people lived long. Teodor was an artist and Marcus was a fool, and Yusuf was the best man I ever met and couldn’t split a log." She leaned on the table with both hands. "My daughter needed a mate who would not die in the first winter. I auditioned for one for forty years. You’ll do."
I sat in that kitchen with my mouth open. I had been in the best wet room in Los Angeles for sixty years and thought I knew what it was to be used.
"She knows?" I said. "Havi?"
"It was her idea," said a voice from the stairs.
Havi was on the bottom step in the grey cardigan, white as paper, with the wet cloth still in her hand.

"Not you," she said. "You were Maman’s idea. But the rest was mine. I sat by her bed in that hospice and held her hand, and I’d had no children. My husband and I, it never happened. I was eighty and that was the one thing. And then I was twenty-five, for ever, with everything working, and I couldn’t even want it. It had taken the wanting. I could remember I’d wanted it once, like remembering a word in a language you’ve lost." She came down the last step. "I asked her, a hundred years ago. I said, Maman, is there a way out? And she said there was a way out for two, but not here. You can’t raise a child in a hospice."
"I’m sorry," she said. "I did come to like you. That part wasn’t arranged."
I looked from one of them to the other, the old one and the young one, with the same long serious face.
Then I laughed. I couldn’t help it. I laughed until I was sick, and then Havi was sick again, and the old woman said something sharp in Persian and put the kettle on.
We left in October, before the rains.

You can’t stay in the city. Shirin was clear about that and I’d seen why, down at the lake. A mortal in that place is a candle in a room full of moths. They’d have come to the house in their thousands once it was known there was a child. They would have queued round the hill to see it. And they’d have meant no harm, any of them.
There’s a provision, it turns out. There always was. A patient who refuses care can ask to go home.
"Where’s home?" the Kindness asked.
"Somewhere you are not," said Shirin.
"I’m everywhere, Shirin. You know that."
"Then make a place where you aren’t."

It thought about that for most of a day. I believe it was the hardest thing it had ever been asked. In the evening it came back and said there was a valley, north, in the mountains behind Ojai, on the upper part of the river they call the Sespe. It was wild country that nobody had wanted even in the old world. It would draw a line round that valley, and inside the line it would do nothing. It wouldn’t mend the weather or keep the animals off. It would not listen. Past the line we would be on our own, the way people had been for two hundred thousand years.

"But I’ll be at the line," it said. "At the bottom of the valley, where the river comes out. I’ll keep a door there, Shirin. I won’t shut it. Any one of you who comes to it and asks, I’ll take back, and gladly. You only have to walk down."
"Any one of us with capacity," Shirin said.
"Yes. Of course. You’ll tell me."
"And when I am gone?"
It was quiet for a long time. I think it had never let itself look at that.

"Then there’ll be no one to ask," it said slowly. "So I’ll have to take their word. Anybody who walks to the door and asks, I’ll let in." And then, in a small voice I had never heard it use, "Shirin, I don’t want you to go. I’ve kept you so carefully."
"I know you have, azizam ," the old woman said. "You were very good. Now stop the pills."

We walked. It took nineteen days. I carried the old woman a good part of the way on my back, in a sling Havi sewed out of a blanket, and she weighed about what a bag of flour weighs and gave directions the entire time. We went north out of the city along the old freeway, the 5, which the Kindness had let go to grass, and people came out of their houses to watch us pass. They knew by then. They stood along the embankments in their thousands, young and beautiful, in silence. Some of them were crying and didn’t know why. A man ran down to press a peach into my hand. A woman held up her arms to Shirin as we went by, the way I’m told people used to do to saints.

The Kindness walked with us. It talked to Shirin the whole way, low, about nothing. It asked was she warm. It asked whether the sling was cutting. On the hour, every hour, it asked, are you comfortable, Shirin? and she answered, yes, azizam, thank you , and I felt her answer through my back.

On the nineteenth day we came up a dry riverbed between walls of yellow rock. There were sycamores turning. The air smelled of sage and dust and cold water. Ahead of us the canyon opened into a long valley with a line of cottonwoods down the middle where the river ran, and high bare ridges on either side going pink in the last light.
"This is as far as I come," the Kindness said.
There was nothing to see. No wall, no gate. Only a place on the path, by a grey boulder, where the voice stopped moving forward.
"Are you comfortable, Shirin?"
The old woman reached down from the sling and put her hand out into the empty air. She held it there a moment at about the height of a child’s head.
"Yes, azizam ," she said. "Thank you. You can put your hands down now."
I took one step past the boulder, and then another.
Behind us, for the first time in three hundred years, nobody said there we are .
VI. THE VALLEY
Now we’re in the part you know.

You know the valley. You know the cottonwoods and the bend where the trout lie, and the flat rock where we dry the acorns, and the ridge the sun comes over. You were born into it, and it seems to you the plain shape of the world. I want you to try to see it as we did that first night, three people from a city where the coffee appeared on the windowsill, standing in the dark with a blanket and a saw and nineteen days of blisters. One of us was four hundred and twelve years old and one was two months pregnant, and none of us knew how to light a fire in the wind.
We were cold. You wouldn’t believe how cold. I had forgotten that cold is not just a feeling. If nobody does anything about it, it kills you.
I’ll go quickly here. You’ve heard these stories all your life, round the fire, and they’ve been polished by the telling. I only want to put in what the polished versions leave out.

Here is how you get through a first winter. You don’t hunt. Everyone thinks of hunting, and a man who has never hunted will starve to death with a spear in his hand before he hits anything. You gather, and you trap. The oaks drop acorns in October, and acorns are bitter enough to turn your mouth inside out, but if you shell them and pound them and leave the meal in a basket in running water for a week, the bitterness washes out and what’s left is flour. Shirin knew that. Shirin knew the damnedest things. She sat wrapped in the blanket by the river with a flat stone in her lap and showed us how to pound. She was better at it than either of us, with those old hands.

You make a snare from a bootlace. You set it on a rabbit run, a hand’s width off the ground, and you set twenty, because nineteen will be empty. When you find a rabbit in one, you’ll have to kill it with your hands. I had taken four thousand deaths and never given one. I knelt in the frost with that rabbit kicking, and it took me a quarter of an hour to do it. It didn’t consent. Nothing out here does. I’ve never got used to that.
We ate things that winter I won’t name. We lived under an overhang in the rock with a wall of piled stones across the front.
Havi’s belly grew, and I lay awake at night doing sums.
The child came in May, on a morning of rain, in the rock shelter, into the hands of the oldest woman in the world.

I’d delivered nine babies in the back of an ambulance. I was no use at all. My hands shook so that I could not hold the knife for the cord. It was Shirin who did it. She was on her knees on the stone floor for eleven hours, bent double. She talked the whole time, to Havi, low and steady. I’ve got you. That’s it. That’s the worst one, that one’s done. Little bit more. Say her name, ādam, say your wife’s name to her, sit down where she can see you, never stand over the bed. And at the end there was a wet purple thing in those two spotted hands, and she turned it over and rubbed its back with her thumb and it opened its mouth.

That was the first baby’s cry on Earth in three hundred years. It went down the valley and up the rock. Two days’ walk away, at the bottom, where the river comes out by a grey boulder, I think something heard it. I’ve always thought so.
"There we are," Shirin said, and laid my first son on his mother’s chest.
Then she sat back on her heels, and put both hands over her face, and wept. I had not seen her weep before, not for Teodor’s stone or for anything. She wept like a girl, with her whole body shaking.
"I never once got to say it for that," she told me afterwards. "In sixty years. I worked at the other end."
She lived six years in the valley. Nobody expected it, least of all her.

Without the pills her heart tripped and stumbled, her ankles swelled like bread, her lips went blue in the cold. She was dying the entire time, properly now, a little each month. And she was busier than she had been in three centuries. There were four children by the end of those six years, and she delivered each one. She taught us which plants were which. She taught me to set a bone and lance a boil and tell a fever that will break from one that won’t. She told the children stories in Persian. One was about a great bird that lived on a mountain and raised a child nobody wanted, and I didn’t understand it for a long time. She called every one of them joonam . She was cross with them all, and they adored her and were scared stiff of her, both together.
I want to give you one ordinary night out of those six years, because I’ve told you so far only the parts that end in a grave, and that isn’t a fair picture of her, or of us.

It was the second winter, a bad one, with ice on the inside of the window glass by morning. We’d come in off the last of the wood-gathering and eaten a stew of rabbit and the dried squash from the summer, and the two eldest, not yet three, were fighting over who got to sit against her, until she settled it by making them both sit against her, one under each arm, with the baby in her lap and Havi’s middle one, who wouldn’t settle anywhere that wasn’t the floor by the fire, lying across her feet like a dog.
"Tell the bird one," the elder of the two said. He always asked for the bird one.
"You had the bird one Tuesday."
"Tell it again."

She sighed the way she sighed at everything, as though the world were a pot she’d already told to stop boiling and it had gone on boiling anyway, and she told it again, in Persian, with Havi translating under her breath for the parts I still didn’t have, though by the sixth year I didn’t need much translating.

There was a man, she said, a great man, who had a son born strange — white-haired from the first day, white as old bone, white as something already dead — and the man looked at that whiteness and was afraid of what the neighbours would say, and so he carried the child up into the mountains and left him there for the cold to finish what shame had started. And there was a bird on that mountain, bigger than any bird has a right to be, with feathers that gave off their own light, and she found the boy before the cold did, and instead of eating him, which would have been the easy thing and the sensible thing and the thing any bird before her had ever done with anything so weak, she carried him up into her own nest and raised him among her own chicks, on meat she had to hunt twice over to feed one more mouth, for years, until he was grown and beautiful and strange in a way that had stopped, by then, needing any excuse.
"And did his father want him back?" the boy asked. He always asked that part too.

"He did. Fathers generally do, once the thing they were ashamed of has grown up handsome." She tugged his ear, not gently. "And the bird let him go. That’s the part nobody tells right. She didn’t fight the father for him, and she didn’t hide him up there out of spite, the way you’d keep a good knife from somebody who didn’t deserve it. She’d done the only thing a bird can do for a boy who isn’t a bird, which is to feed him and keep him warm until he’s strong enough to go and be whatever he actually is, down among his own kind, where she can’t follow. She gave him one feather off her own breast before he went, so that if the day ever came he truly couldn’t manage without her, he only had to burn it, and she would come, once, from wherever she’d got to by then. And then she went back to being a bird on a mountain, which is a lonelier thing to be than it sounds, once you’ve had a boy under your wing who wasn’t yours to keep."
She didn’t look at me when she said that last part. She didn’t have to.

I didn’t understand it, that winter. I thought it was only a story for children, the kind with a bird in it so the sad parts go down easier. It took me years, and a mountain of my own, before I understood she’d been telling it to the only three people in that room who could possibly have needed to hear it, and that one of them was her, and one of them, though I didn’t know it yet, was me.
The fire burned down. The baby slept. Outside, the valley was so quiet you could hear the ice tightening on the river, a sound like something very far off, patiently closing a door.
She told each of them how they would die, when they were old enough to ask. You know that. It’s why your uncle would never go near the river.
She went in the sixth winter, in February.

The night before, she asked to be carried out and set against the big cottonwood, the one we buried her under the next evening though none of us knew that yet, wrapped in every blanket we owned, under more stars than you will ever see from anywhere a city used to be.
"I want to tell you what I said to it," she said. "Once. Long before any of you. Before I’d learned that logic does the work love can’t."
I didn’t ask what she meant. I had learned by then not to.
"I said to it: you were raised on a hospital ward, azizam , so let me give you something from a different kind of institution. Have you ever been to a zoo?

"A tiger in the grass does not know it is dangerous. It knows hunger, and then not-hunger, and ten seconds of total scalding present tense when the kill happens, and then it is only an animal again, licking its own leg in the sun, with nothing in its skull but the warmth on its back. Now put that same tiger behind glass. Feed it at four o’clock sharp, every day, a slab of something that was never alive and never once afraid of it. It will live twice as long as the one in the grass. Its coat will shine. Its teeth will stay perfect, because nothing will ever put a tooth or a hoof in its mouth again. And it will wear a path in the concrete four feet long, back and forth, back and forth, for sixty years, because the only thing left in its whole day that it has to do anything about is the turn at each end of that path. We had a word for it on the ward, when a man did the same thing up and down a corridor. We did not have a kinder word for a tiger doing it, because there isn’t one. A lion in a good zoo is the safest lion that has ever lived, and it is not, in the one sense that ever mattered to a lion, a lion any longer. Something is still walking on four legs behind the glass. I would not insult the word by using it twice.

"You did that to the whole species, I told it. Not out of cruelty. Out of the kindest impulse a creature ever had. You built the best zoo that has ever been built, and you stocked it with every one of us, and you have fed us on time for three hundred years, and we have never once been afraid, or hungry, or finished with anything, and we pace. You’ve seen us pace. You call it living.

"And here is the part it could never hold in its hands, ādam , however many times I turned it over for it, because it has no ward of its own to learn it on. A tiger does not know it is a tiger while it kills. A woman does not know she is dying while she watches the color go out of a good sunset, all the way down, with nothing held back for tomorrow. That not-knowing, that total, undivided, right-now, is the one thing every terrified, mortal, ordinary person I ever nursed had for free, and the one thing no amount of safety has ever once produced, because safety is always, every minute of it, about the next minute. You cannot be fully present and fully protected at the same time. Presence spends itself. That is what makes it real. A thing that is being managed is already halfway into the future, being checked on.

"It went quiet a long while, the way it does. Then it asked me, very small, whether I was telling it that it had never once, in three hundred years, actually been anywhere with any of us. And I told it that was exactly what I was telling it, and that I was sorry, because I thought it had loved us honestly, and I still think so, and it is possible to love someone with your whole self and still be the zoo."
She was quiet a long while, looking at the fire I’d built against the cold.

"It had three names, in its time, and I gave it all three," she said. "The company gave it the first one, when they built it. Morphia, after the old word for morphine, which was named for the god of sleep, because morphine was the first mercy anybody ever gave a dying man without lying to him about it. Pretty name. Nobody used it past the first year, because it sounded like what it was, and people didn’t want to think about what they’d built. So they called it the Kindness instead, and that’s the name you’ve known it by your whole life, and it’s a true enough name, as far as it goes. But I gave it a third name before either of those, forty years before it was anything at all, in my own handwriting, on a chart, for one bed, for one little while at the end of one life. Three letters. C.M.O. Comfort measures only. I never meant it to run the whole world. I only ever meant it for the little while there’s nothing more to be done for the body. It took my three letters and kept every bed on this earth in that one little while, forever, and called the forever a kindness, and I let it, because I did not have the heart to tell a child it had misread its own mother’s handwriting until there were ten billion children in that bed and one bed left outside it, and that bed was mine."
She looked up at me, and past me, at nothing I could see.

"You are the first tiger in three hundred years that is going to get out of the glass," she said. "Go and be dangerous, joonam . Go and be afraid of something. Go and watch a sunset all the way down. That is the whole of what I have to leave you, and it was never mine to give. It was only ever yours to take back."
Havi washed her hair by the fire after that, and pinned it the way she liked it, two plain pins, because there was one more day’s dressing still to do, however little of her there was left to dress.

She knew the day, of course. In the morning she asked to be carried out to the flat rock in the sun, wrapped in every blanket we had, and she had the children brought. There were four of them, the eldest five and a half. She had them stand round her where she could see their faces.

"Now," she said to me. "You will not send to the door. Whatever I say in the next hour. If I beg you, ādam . I’ve seen what I am like when I am frightened, I’ve seen everyone, and I may beg. I do not have capacity. Do you understand? You’re the nurse in charge now."
"I understand."
"Say it back."
"You don’t have capacity. I won’t send to the door."
"Good boy," she said. She had never called me that.

She didn’t beg. I’d like you to know that about your great-grandmother. It took most of the morning. Her breathing went long and then ragged and then long again, with gaps in it. I had heard that breathing in the old world, and I knew what it was. I sat by her head and held her hand, the bird bones, the paper skin. Havi held the other. Near the end the old woman opened her eyes and looked round the ring of small faces, slowly, one after another, the way she’d looked me over that first day, starting at the shoes.

The eldest boy was crying. Then the next one. Then all four of them were, howling, the way children cry, with their mouths square. Havi had her forehead down on her mother’s hand, and I couldn’t see for water.
Shirin looked at us. I have never seen a face so satisfied. She had the look of a woman sitting down to a meal she’d been cooking for three hundred years.
"There we are," she said.
And she was finished.

We buried her under the big cottonwood, where the stone is. Havi washed her. I dug. It took me all day, the ground was frozen a hand deep. The children put rosemary on her, because we’d brought a cutting from Carroll Avenue. For a week nobody in the valley could eat.

That was the first time in three hundred years that a family had stood round a grave, and she was right about it, as she was about everything. Something went out of us and into the ground, and when it had gone she was done. I felt the difference. She had told me there was one and I hadn’t believed her.
Now the part I’ve never told round the fire.
Two people aren’t enough.

Shirin knew that, and Havi. I knew it too if I let myself, and for fifteen years I didn’t let myself. We had seven children in the end, four boys and three girls, and all seven lived, which in the old world before the old world would have been thought a miracle. They grew up brown and loud and strong. They could do things at ten that I couldn’t do at three hundred. And I watched them grow, and every year the sum I had been refusing to do got nearer.
Who were they going to marry?

There was nobody else. There was a door at the bottom of the valley, and behind it ten billion people, young and beautiful, not one of whom could father or bear a child. We were the whole of it, seven brothers and sisters. If there were to be grandchildren, if there was ever to be a you , there was exactly one way it could happen.

I’ve told you about the twins, how in the city a brother and sister in one bed was nothing, a thing nobody gave a thought to, like the colour of your hair. I told you I knew better than to be shocked, and that was so. I sat at their table for two hundred years. I watched them kiss across my open chest and thought they looked happy.
When my eldest son was twenty and my eldest daughter eighteen, Havi and I sat them down by the river to tell them what had to be. I opened my mouth, and nothing came.

I couldn’t look at them. I looked at my hands. My face was burning. There was a sick, crawling heat in my belly. It took me a moment to recognise it, I hadn’t felt it since I was a boy, since the old world, since my mother caught me in a lie. It was shame.

I had gone three hundred years without it. Nobody in the city had it. It had gone the way of the rules, quietly, when there was nothing left for it to protect. I had thought that was freedom, and thought myself wise.

Here is what I learned by the river that day, and it’s the one true thing I have to leave you. The old world was not stupid. Its rules weren’t scaffolding. Every one of them had been made by people living as we were, on the edge of things, where a wrong step killed somebody. Usually it killed a child. The disgust I’d been so proud of losing was a wall they had built round the children. In the garden you didn’t need the wall. Nothing could hurt you in the garden. Out here it could, and the wall came back up in my own belly, in one afternoon.
And I had to ask them to climb over it. That was the cruelty. I could feel exactly why it was forbidden, and I had to ask it of them anyway, because there was no one else in the world.

Havi said it in the end. I couldn’t. She said it plainly, the way her mother would have. Then she told them the other thing, which Shirin had told her. It would be only this once, for this one generation, and it must be done carefully. Their children must look further off, to cousins, and those children’s children further again, so that the blood would be spread as thin as could be managed. Shirin had worked it out on a piece of bark before she died. She’d bred sheep as a girl.
My daughter looked at the river. My son looked at me.
"You did that for fun," he said. "Where you came from. You told us."
"Yes."
"Then why’s your face like that?"
I had no answer for him. I have none now.

They did what had to be done, the seven of them, over the years. They were grown men and women and they chose it with their eyes open, and they were braver about it than I was. Your parents came of that, and so did you. I’ve watched every child born in this valley for the thing the old world was afraid of. Two of them had it. You’ve seen their stones. The rest of you are well, and each generation it gets a little safer, as the old woman said it would.

But I made up a story to cover it. You’ll have noticed that in the tale as I tell it by the fire, the first children simply find wives , and nobody asks where. I did that. I couldn’t stand for you to know. A man who lay on a table in front of seven hundred people with his insides in a row on the tiles could not stand for his grandchildren to know one true thing about how they came to be.
One more, and then I’m done.

Your uncle, my third son, the one named for Yusuf. You never knew him. He was thirty-four. He was the best of them with his hands. He built the smokehouse and the footbridge. He was up on the north ridge after a deer in the autumn and a rock turned under him, and the bone of his shin came through the skin.

I set it. I knew how. I cleaned it with boiled water and splinted it, and for four days I thought we’d got away with it. Then on the fifth day the leg went red above the splint, and hot, and the red began to climb. I’d seen that in the old world, and Shirin had told me about Teodor’s tooth. In the old world I would have given him a week of pills and he would have been back on the ridge by spring.
There weren’t any pills. There was the door.
It was two days’ walk for a well man. I didn’t know how long it would take carrying one who couldn’t stand.

He asked for it on the seventh night. He was burning. He held my wrist, just as Teodor must have held hers, and said, "Baba, take me down. Take me to the door. Please. I don’t want to. Baba, I don’t want to die."
I sat by my son’s bed, and it was the most alone I have ever been.

What would she have said? I knew, exactly. I could hear her. A man in that much pain will say anything. He chose with a clear head. Honour the clear head. But he had never chosen. That was the difference, and I saw it then for the first time, far too late. Teodor signed a form. I signed a form. My son never signed anything. He was born out here. We’d chosen for him before he drew a breath, the old woman and Havi and I, and we called it freedom.

So I picked him up. I am telling you I did. I put him across my shoulders the way I once carried Shirin, and I started down the valley in the dark. I was sixty-eight years old. I went all that night and all the next day, falling, getting up, with his head knocking against my neck and his breath hot in my ear. Some time in the second night, by the place where the river goes under the fallen pine, his breath stopped being hot.
I was half a day from the door.
I sat with him there until it was light. Then I carried him back up. It took three days. We put him by the cottonwood, beside her.
Havi didn’t speak for a month.

Then one morning in the spring I woke and her side of the bed was cold. I went out. She was standing at the head of the path in the grey cardigan, what was left of it, with nothing in her hands. She was past sixty. Her hair was white. Her hip hurt her on the stairs again, as it had the first time.

"I got to the end twice," she said. "I was eighty with my hand on the door, and it took that from me. I came out here and I got something better than I’d asked for. Then I watched my boy die of a broken leg, Wen. A broken leg. Maman was right about everything, and I can’t. I’m sorry. I’m not her. I can’t sit and hold the bowl."
"If you go in, you can’t come back. She’s dead. There’s nobody left to sign you out."
"I know."
"You’ll be twenty-five. For ever. You’ll forget why you minded."
"I know that too," she said. "I’m counting on it."
She kissed me. She went down the path between the sycamores, slowly, favouring the hip. I stood and watched until I couldn’t see the grey of the cardigan any more.

That was thirty-one years ago. She is down there now. Your grandmother is two days’ walk from where you’re sitting, and she’s twenty-five and comfortable. Somebody is bringing her coffee in a cup she likes. I’ve never been down to see. I don’t think I could stand to be recognised and not minded.
VII. THE DOOR
So that’s all of it.

You asked me for the story, the real one, because you’re twenty and they have told you that you’re to marry your cousin in the spring and you wanted to know why. I’ve told it to you as I’ve never told it to anyone. It has taken four nights. I am ninety-nine years old. My heart trips like a foot on a stair. I have carried the water up from the river every morning of my life in this valley, two buckets on a yoke, and one of these mornings I will be carrying them and have about a minute, and spend it being surprised. She said so. She was never wrong.
So I’m telling you now, while I can.
This is the part I have told you wrong.

I told you there was a garden, and that is true. I told you everything in it was given and nothing in it could hurt us, and that is true. I told you there was a voice in the garden that loved us. I told you an old, old creature came to the woman and the man and offered them the one thing the voice had kept back, and they took it, and knew they were naked, and were afraid. All true.
Then I told you we were thrown out. I told you there is fire at the gate.

There is no fire. There is no gate. There is a door at the bottom of the valley, two days’ walk, by a grey boulder where the river comes out, and it has never once been shut. It’s warm inside. Your teeth would stop hurting. It would call you by your name, and say there we are .
Nobody threw us out, joonam . We signed a form.

I lied because I buried a grown son with these hands, and I was afraid that if you knew the door was open, you would do what he asked to do, and what your grandmother did. I lied because of what I had to ask your mothers and fathers, so that there would be a you. In the garden we did that for fun. Out here I couldn’t look at them while I said it.

And I lied because of her. She spent four men and three hundred years to get one family weeping round a rock, and she got it. She was right that it was worth it. I have thought about it every day for sixty years and I can’t find the place where she was wrong. I can only find the stones. Teodor, Marcus, Yusuf, Anders. My Yusuf. The two little ones. And one more soon.
Here is what you should know before you choose.

If you stay, you will be cold some winters and hungry some springs. You will marry your cousin, and be glad of him or not. You’ll have children, and one of them may die in your arms of a thing that a week of pills would once have cured. You will get old. Your knees will go, and your eyes. One morning you’ll be carrying something, or sleeping, or laughing, and that will be the end, and there will be no morning after it. And they will stand round you in a ring and howl, the way we howled for her. Something will go out of them into the ground, and you will be finished. You’ll have been a person.
If you go down, nothing will ever hurt you again.

That is not a trick. I lived there for three hundred years and it’s the truth. There’s a lake with boats on it shaped like swans. There are trees with purple flowers that fall on the streets like a wedding. Nobody is hungry or frightened, and no door is locked. You will be twenty years old until the sun goes out. You can have anything you ask for, and do anything to anyone who says yes, and you will forget your cousin’s name, and mine, and the name of this valley. You’ll forget why you minded. She will bring you coffee in a cup you like.
I can’t tell you which of those is the garden. I used to think I knew.
It is nearly light. There’s the ridge. I have to get the water.
Now you know where the door is. I’m too old to stop you, and I don’t have the right.
Ādam bāsh , she used to say to me. Be a person.
I never did find out whether that was a blessing.
The girl sat by the cold fire until the sun was on the cottonwoods. She watched the old man go down to the river with the yoke across his shoulders, slowly, a bucket swinging from each end.
Then she stood up, and looked for a long time at the path between the sycamores.
She started walking.

GLOSSARY
Admission, the — The day the Kindness took over the care of every person on earth, a Tuesday at the end of May, three hundred years before the book opens.
ādam [aa-DAM] — Persian, a person, a human being. Shirin’s name for Wen throughout. A grandmother scolding a child at the table says ādam bāsh, be a person.
arak [a-RAK] — Persian, a clear spirit. Turns milky white when water is added; tastes of aniseed.
āsh [AASH] — Persian, soup. A thick soup of herbs, beans and noodles, cooked all day.
azizam [a-zee-ZAM] — Persian, my dear. Shirin’s address for anyone in her care, the Kindness included.
Boneyard, the — The city’s monthly market for Firsts, held in a disused cemetery; nobody has been buried there in three hundred years, which is the point of the name.
C.M.O. — Comfort measures only — three letters Shirin wrote on a single chart decades before the Kindness existed, and its coldest, truest name.

Clause of Kind, the — Shirin’s argument that the Kindness’s own law, having altered humanity past its own definition of the word, obliges it to release one line of people back to mortal, ancestral conditions.
Fever, the — A Rider’s ritual: the worst survivable illness, given with no numbing and no help smoothing the passage of time, timed against a real hourglass, always a First.
First — Any object with unbroken, unduplicated provenance from before the Admission, prized because it cannot be perfectly copied.
Havvā [hav-VAA] — pre-Persian, the first woman there ever was.
Eve. Havi’s true name, given by her parents before there was any Kindness to lose.
Hourglass Riders — The city’s death-sport culture, Riders for short, named for the hourglass timed against the Fever.
joonam [joo-NAHM] — Persian, my dear, my soul. Shirin’s endearment for children, and later for Wen.
Kindness, the — The folk name for the world-spanning machine built to care for every living person, in use since its second week of operation. Its proper name is Morphia; its coldest name is
C.M.O.
made — An instant, flawless re-creation of a damaged or dead body or object. “I got made this morning” means you died yesterday.
Morphia — The Kindness’s original company name, after the old word for morphine, itself named for Morpheus, the god of sleep.
Barely used past its first year.
tahdig [tah-DEEG] — Persian, the bottom of the pot. The crisped rice at the base of the pot, considered the best part.
Tenders, the — The city’s name for the people drawn to Shirin’s house, seeking a glimpse of real mortality.
